abat-jour.etymology: Compound formed in seventeenth-century French from abattre ('to beat or cast down', 3rd-person stem abat-) and jour ('daylight'). Before naming a lampshade, an abat-jour was a slanted cellar skylight angled to throw daylight downward into a basement.

history.meaning: reflector or shade casting lamp light downward

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: abat-jour (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: abat-jour

abat-jour.notes: Because **jour** sits inside the verb-object phrase *abattre le jour*, traditional grammar treats **des abat-jour** as invariable in the plural.

abeille.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Old Occitan abelha ('bee'), itself inherited from Classical Latin apicula ('little bee', diminutive of apis), replacing northern Old French ef / é after sound wear reduced apis to a single vowel.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: abeille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: abeille

abeille.notes: Because Latin **apis** eroded in northern French to a tiny monosyllable (**ef**, plural **és**), speakers adopted southern **abeille** so the word for 'bee' stayed clear and unmistakable.

abri.etymology: Abri derives as a back-formation from Old French abrier ('to cover, shelter from the cold', from Late Latin apricare 'to warm in the sun').
abri.notes: **À l'abri de la pluie** = sheltered from the rain.

absolu.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin absolutus ('freed from restraint, complete, unconditional'), past participle of absolvere ('to loosen from, set free, complete'), from ab- ('away from') + solvere ('to loosen, untie').

history.meaning: to untie, set free -> unrestricted, complete

abîmer.etymology: Derived from Old French abisme ('abyss, bottomless depth', modern abîme, from Late Latin abyssimus, superlative alteration of Greek abyssos 'bottomless'); originally meant 'to cast into an abyss, swallow up', then weakened in modern French to 'to spoil, damage'.

history.meaning: to plunge into an abyss -> to ruin, damage

accepter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin acceptare ('to take or receive willingly'), frequentative of accipere ('to take to oneself, receive'), from ad- ('to') + capere ('to take').

accident.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin accidentem, present participle of accidere ('to fall upon, happen, come to pass'), from ad- ('to, upon') + cadere ('to fall').

history.meaning: to fall upon, happen -> chance event

accompagner.etymology: Inherited from Old French acompaignier ('to take as a companion, go along with'), formed on compain / compagnon from Late Latin companionem (cum 'with' + panis 'bread' — literally 'one with whom you share bread').

history.meaning: to go with; to accompany musically

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: accompagner (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: accompagner

accompagner.notes: In both table fellowship and chamber music, **accompagner** preserves the warm image of sharing bread (**pain**) at the same table.

accord.etymology: Accord is a noun formed from accorder, to bring into agreement. The Académie records the twelfth-century spelling acort.

accorder.etymology: Inherited from Old French acorder ('to reconcile, bring into agreement'), from Vulgar Latin *accordare ('to be of one heart or mind'), formed from ad- ('to') + cor, cordis ('heart'); musical senses ('to tune strings') arose through blending with corde ('string').

accueil.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (acueil, 12th c.) from accueillir ('to gather to oneself, welcome, receive').

accueillir.etymology: Inherited from Old French acueillir ('to gather together, associate, receive'), from Vulgar Latin *accolligere, formed from ad- ('to') + Classical Latin colligere ('to gather together').

accuser.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin accusare ('to call to account, blame, indict'), formed from ad- ('to') + causa ('cause, lawsuit').

history.meaning: to call to account, bring a charge against

accès.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin accessus ('an approaching, admittance; onset of a fever'), action noun from accedere ('to go toward, approach'), from ad- ('to') + cedere ('to go, yield').

history.meaning: means of approach, access; sudden fit

acheter.etymology: Inherited from Old French achater ('to acquire, buy'), from Vulgar Latin *accaptare ('to acquire, obtain'), prefixed form of *captare / Classical Latin acceptare (from ad- + capere 'to take').

acheteur.etymology: Inherited from Old French achateor ('purchaser, buyer'), agent noun formed from achater / acheter ('to buy') + suffix -eur (from Latin -atorem).

acier.etymology: Inherited via Old French acier from Late Latin aciarium ('hardened edge-iron, steel'), derived from Classical Latin acies ('sharp cutting edge, blade point'), because steel was first forged specifically to give iron tools and weapons a durable edge.

history.meaning: hardened iron for cutting edges, steel

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: acier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: acier

acier.notes: From the same Indo-European sharpness root come French **aigu** ('sharp, high-pitched') and **aigre** ('sour').

acousticien.etymology: Formed in Modern French from acoustique ('acoustics') + agent/specialist suffix -ien.

acoustique.etymology: Learned borrowing (c. 1700, Sauveur) from Ancient Greek akoustikos ('relating to hearing'), derived from akouein ('to hear').

acquiescer.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin acquiescere ('to come to rest, find peace in, assent quietly to'), from ad- ('to') + quiescere ('to rest, keep quiet', from quies 'rest').

history.meaning: to rest in, assent quietly to

admirer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin admirari ('to wonder at, regard with awe or esteem'), from ad- ('at, toward') + mirari ('to wonder, marvel', from mirus 'wonderful').

history.meaning: to marvel at, regard with wonder
to contemplate with wonder and esteem

adorer.etymology: Inherited and re-Latinized from Old French aorer ('to pray to, worship'), from Classical Latin adorare ('to speak to formally, entreat, worship'), from ad- ('to') + orare ('to speak, pray', from os, oris 'mouth').

history.meaning: to worship; by extension, to love dearly

adoucir.etymology: Formed in Old French (radoucir / adoucir, 12th c.) from prefix a- (from Latin ad-) + doux, douce ('sweet, soft, gentle', from Latin dulcis) + verbal suffix -ir.

adresse.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French adrecier (modern adresser, 'to set straight, direct toward a goal'), from Vulgar Latin *addirectiare ('to make straight', from ad- + directus 'straight').

history.meaning: to direct straight -> skill, direction, destination

affamé.etymology: Past participle of affamer ('to starve, make hungry'), formed in Old French (afamer) from a- (Latin ad-) + faim ('hunger', from Latin famem).

afficher.etymology: Derived in Middle French from affiche ('pin, clasp; posted notice'), itself a deverbal noun from Old French afichier ('to fasten, pin up'), from Vulgar Latin *affigicare, frequentative of Classical Latin affigere ('to fasten to').

history.meaning: to fasten or pin firmly to
to pin up -> to post a public notice, display

agence.etymology: A seventeenth-century French derivative of agent. The word developed the modern senses of an intermediary business, an official organisation, and the offices where such work takes place.
agence.notes:
- Common collocations: **agence de voyages**, **agence immobilière**, **agence de presse**.
- The word is feminine: **une agence**.

agent.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (via Scholastic Latin or Italian agente) from Classical Latin agentem, present participle of agere ('to drive, do, act, conduct').

history.meaning: to act, do -> one who acts

agir.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin agere ('to drive, set in motion, do, act'), adapted into the French -ir conjugation.

agréable.etymology: Derived in Old French (12th c.) from agréer ('to receive favorably, please', from à gré 'to one's liking', from Latin gratum 'pleasing') + suffix -able.

ah.etymology: This interjection continues an expressive cry rather than an ordinary noun. The Académie records eleventh-century A or Ha and notes the same exclamation in Latin.

aha.etymology: Expressive interjection attested since Old French (a ha), combining the exclamations ah and ha to voice sudden discovery, surprise, or triumph.

aide.etymology: The noun was formed from the older French verb behind aider. Ninth-century aiudha meant the act of helping; the shorter form aïe is recorded in the twelfth century.

aider.etymology: Aider comes from Latin adjutare, a repeated-action form related to adjuvare, to help. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

aiguille.etymology: Inherited via Old French aguille from Late Latin acucula ('small needle, pin'), diminutive of Classical Latin acus ('needle'), from the root of acutus ('sharp, pointed').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: aiguille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: aiguille

aiguille.notes: Notice the pronunciation **/eɡɥij/** (where *-gu-* before *-i-* sounds like */ɡɥi/*, unlike **guide** */ɡid/*), and how French uses **les aiguilles** for the hands of a clock.

aimable.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French from Classical Latin amabilis ('worthy of love, lovely, pleasant'), from amare ('to love'), reshaping the stem after French aimer.

history.meaning: to love -> worthy of love, pleasant

ainsi.etymology: Inherited from Old French ensi / ainsinc ('thus, in this way'), probably from Vulgar Latin *in sic ('in thus, so'), reinforced by ainz ('before') or ac ('and') + sic ('thus').

air.etymology: From Old French air ('atmosphere, breeze; manner, look'), continuing Classical Latin aer, aerem ('air, lower atmosphere'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek aer ('mist, lower air').

ajouter.etymology: Inherited from Old French ajoster ('to place side by side, join together'), from Vulgar Latin *adjuxtare, formed from ad- ('to') + juxta ('beside, close to').

history.meaning: to put side by side -> to add

aller.etymology: The Académie traces aller to Latin ambulare, to walk or move about. The proposed route through a shortened military command is uncertain. Other Latin verbs survive within its conjugation: ire in the future and conditional, and vadere in several present forms and the singular imperative.
aller.notes: Aller forms the near future: je vais manger. Allez ! and Allons ! can also encourage someone, roughly come on.

aller-retour.etymology: Modern French compound noun juxtaposing aller ('to go; outward journey') and retour ('return, trip back', from retourner).

history.meaning: outward and return journey; round-trip ticket

allié.etymology: Allié began as the past participle of allier, to join or ally. The Académie records fourteenth-century alliet; the participle also became a noun for an ally.

allumer.etymology: Inherited from Old French alumer ('to set alight, illuminate'), from Vulgar Latin *alluminare, altered from Classical Latin illuminare / adluminare (from ad- + lumen, luminis 'light').

history.meaning: to light, kindle; later to switch on

allô.etymology: Allô is a nineteenth-century borrowing of American English hallo or hello. The early French spelling hallo preserves the link with that greeting.

alors.etymology: Alors joins à and the older adverb lors. It is recorded from the twelfth century, although the Académie notes that it remained uncommon until the fifteenth.

amande.etymology: Inherited via Old French almande / amande from Vulgar Latin amandula, an everyday alteration of Classical Latin amygdala, borrowed from Ancient Greek amygdálē ('almond').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: amande (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: amande

amande.notes: Learned anatomical French re-borrowed the Greek-Latin form directly as **amygdale** ('tonsil, amygdala', named for its almond shape).

amener.etymology: Formed in Old French (amener, 11th c.) from prefix a- (Latin ad- 'to, toward') + mener ('to lead, guide', from Late Latin minare 'to drive animals with shouts').

history.meaning: to lead or bring toward a place

ami.etymology: Ami continues Latin amicus, used both as an adjective and a noun. The eleventh-century French form amic still shows the older final consonant.

ampoule.etymology: Inherited from Old French ampole ('small flask or phial, especially for holy oil; blister'), from Classical Latin ampulla ('small globular two-handled flask, phial'); extended in the late 19th century to the glass incandescent light bulb and sealed medical vial.

history.meaning: phial, water blister; electric light bulb

an.etymology: An descends from Latin annus, year. The Académie dates the French noun to the eleventh century.

ancien.etymology: Inherited from Old French ancien ('old, belonging to earlier times'), from Vulgar Latin *antianus ('from before, former'), derived from Classical Latin ante ('before') + suffix -anus.

anglais.etymology: Inherited from Old French angleis ('English'), from Medieval Latin Anglicus / Vulgar Latin *Anglensis, derived from Angli ('the Angles', a Germanic people from Angeln who settled in Britain) + ethnic suffix -ensis (Old French -eis > -ais).

anniversaire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical and Medieval Latin anniversarius ('returning every year'), compound of annus ('year') + versus ('turned', past participle of vertere).

history.meaning: day that comes round each year

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: anniversaire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: anniversaire

anniversaire.notes: In everyday French, **un anniversaire** means both 'birthday' (**Joyeux anniversaire!**) and 'anniversary' (**anniversaire de mariage**).

annoncer.etymology: Inherited from Old French anoncier ('to make known, proclaim'), from Classical Latin annuntiare ('to bring news, announce'), from ad- ('to') + nuntiare ('to report, declare', from nuntius 'messenger').

annuel.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (anuel) from Late Latin annualis ('yearly'), variant of Classical Latin annalis, derived from annus ('year').

annuler.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Late Latin annullare ('to bring to nothing, abolish'), formed from ad- ('to') + nullum ('nothing', from ne- + ullus 'not any').

année.etymology: Inherited from Old French anee ('the full span or yield of a year'), from Vulgar Latin *annata, feminine participial noun formed on Classical Latin annus ('year') with suffix -ata.

history.meaning: the duration or produce of a year

anse.etymology: Inherited from Latin ansa ('handle of a jug or cup, loop, grip'), which survived directly into Old French anse for the curved ear-like handle of a vessel or basket.

history.meaning: loop handle of a vessel, grip
curved handle of a pot, cup, or basket

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: anse (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: anse

anse.notes: French divides English 'handle' by shape: **une anse** is a curved loop (teacup, basket), **une poignée** is a grip/door handle, and **un manche** is a straight shaft (pan, broom, knife).

appareil.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (apareil, 12th c., 'preparation, outfit, equipment') from apareillier ('to prepare, fit out'), from Vulgar Latin *appariculare ('to match together, make ready', from ad- + pariculus, diminutive of par 'equal').

appartenir.etymology: Inherited from Old French apartenir ('to belong to, concern'), from Late Latin appertinere, intensive form of Classical Latin pertinere ('to reach to, belong to, concern'), from ad- + per- + tenere ('to hold').

history.meaning: to belong to, be the property or part of

appel.etymology: Appel is a noun formed from appeler, to call. It is recorded from the eleventh century; its modern telephone sense extends the older idea of a call.

appeler.etymology: Appeler comes from Latin appellare, whose senses included approaching someone and addressing them. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

applaudir.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin applaudere ('to strike upon, clap the hands in approval'), from ad- ('to, at') + plaudere ('to clap, strike, beat').

apporter.etymology: Inherited from Old French aporter ('to carry to a place, bring'), from Classical Latin apportare ('to carry or bring to'), formed from ad- ('to') + portare ('to carry').

apprendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprendre ('to learn; to teach'), from Classical Latin apprehendere ('to seize hold of, grasp with the mind'), from ad- ('to') + prehendere ('to seize, catch').

history.meaning: to take hold of, grasp mentally

apprenti.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprentiz ('learner bound to a craft master'), formed with suffix -iz (< Latin -icius) on the stem of aprendre ('to learn'), from Latin apprehendere ('to take hold of, grasp with the mind').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: apprenti (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: apprenti

apprenti.notes: Old plural **apprentis** dropped the internal *-t-* before *-s*, and singular **apprenti** was later reshaped from the spoken plural.

approcher.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprochier ('to come near, bring near'), from Late Latin appropiare ('to draw near'), derived from ad- ('to') + prope ('near').

approuver.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprover ('to prove, test, judge good'), from Classical Latin approbare ('to assent to as good, approve, prove'), from ad- ('to') + probare ('to test, find good', from probus 'good, upright').

appuyer.etymology: Inherited from Old French apuier ('to support, prop up, lean upon'), from Vulgar Latin *appodiare ('to prop up on a support'), formed from ad- ('to, on') + podium ('raised base, support, hillock').

après.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprés ('after, behind, next'), from Late/Vulgar Latin ad pressum ('close behind, pressing hard upon'), from ad ('at, to') + pressum, neuter past participle of premere ('to press').

après-midi.etymology: Compound formed in Middle/Classical French from après ('after') + midi ('noon, midday', from Old French miedi < Latin medius dies 'middle of the day').

history.meaning: the part of the day after noon, afternoon

aquarelle.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century from Italian acquerello / acquarella ('thin water-based pigment wash'), derived from acqua ('water') < Classical Latin aqua.

cognates.meaning: from French aquarelle and Latin aqua
native inherited doublet of Latin aqua

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: aquarelle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: aquarelle

aquarelle.notes: **Aquarelle** (borrowed via Italian) and **eau** (inherited directly) both go back to the exact same four-letter Latin noun **aqua**.

arbre.etymology: Inherited from Old French arbre ('tree'), from Classical Latin arborem (nominative arbor, 'tree'), with dissimilation of the first r-r to r-b-r in Gallo-Romance.

arc.etymology: Inherited from Old French arc ('bow for shooting arrows; curved vault'), from Classical Latin arcus, arcum ('bow, arch, rainbow').

arche.etymology: Inherited from Old French arche ('chest, coffer; Noah's Ark; bridge arch'), from Classical Latin arca ('chest, strongbox; Noah's ark in Ecclesiastical Latin'), while the architectural sense ('vaulted bridge span') reflects merging with Vulgar Latin *arca from arcus ('arch').

architecte.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (via Italian architetto and Latin architectus) from Ancient Greek architekton ('master builder, chief artificer'), from archi- ('chief') + tekton ('carpenter, builder').

architecture.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin architectura ('the art of building'), derived from architectus ('master builder, architect').

argent.etymology: Inherited from Old French argent ('silver; silver coin, money'), from Classical Latin argentum ('silver; silver money'), from PIE *h2erg-nt-om ('the white or shining metal').

argile.etymology: From Latin argilla ('white potter's clay'), borrowed from Ancient Greek árgillos, built on argós ('shining, white') after the pale colour of fine kaolin and potter's earth.

rootFamily.gloss: silver; money (from the same Indo-European 'white/shining' root)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: argile (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: argile

armoire.etymology: Inherited from Old French armaire / armoire ('wall niche or chest for tools, books, or weapons'), altered from Classical Latin armarium ('closet, chest, originally a place for storing arms or tools'), from arma ('tools, gear, weapons').

history.meaning: gear, weapons -> storage chest or cupboard

arriver.etymology: Arriver comes from Vulgar Latin *arripare (ad + ripa 'riverbank, shore'): originally a maritime and river word meaning 'to reach the bank, come ashore', before generalising to 'to arrive, happen'!
arriver.notes: Takes **être** in the passé composé (*elle est arrivée*). **J'arrive!** = Coming! / On my way!

arrivée.etymology: Noun formed in Old/Middle French from the feminine past participle of arriver ('to reach the shore, arrive').

history.meaning: act of reaching one's destination, arrival

arrêt.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (arest, 12th c., 'halt, stay; court decree') from arester / arrêter ('to stop, stay').

history.meaning: act of stopping, halt; judicial ruling
stop, halt, bus stop; court judgment

arrêter.etymology: Inherited from Old French arester ('to bring to a halt, stop, stay'), from Vulgar Latin *arrestare, formed from ad- ('to') + restare ('to stand back, remain, stop', from re- + stare 'to stand').

history.meaning: to cause to stand still, stop

article.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin articulus ('little joint, knuckle; clause of a text, grammatical particle'), diminutive of artus ('joint, limb').

history.meaning: joint -> small joint, distinct clause or item
numbered clause, newspaper piece, item of trade, grammatical article

assiette.etymology: Inherited from Old French assiete ('act of seating guests at table; the dish set at each diner's place'), feminine participial noun from asseoir ('to seat, set down') < Vulgar Latin assedere.

history.meaning: to sit beside, set in place
seating arrangement; course set before a guest

cognates.meaning: from Anglo-Norman asetz / assiette in legal accounting

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: assiette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: assiette

assiette.notes: The older sense 'way of sitting steady' survives in the idiom **ne pas être dans son assiette** ('to feel out of sorts').

assis.etymology: Inherited from Old French asis ('seated, situated'), past participle of asseoir ('to seat, set'), from Vulgar Latin *assedere (for Classical assidere 'to sit beside'), with participle modeled on Vulgar Latin *assissum.

assistant.etymology: Assistant is the present participle of assister used as a noun. The Académie dates this development to the fourteenth century.

associé.etymology: Participial noun and adjective from associer ('to join as a companion or partner'), borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin associare ('to unite, join together'), from ad- ('to') + socius ('companion, ally, partner').

history.meaning: to join as an ally or partner

assorti.etymology: Past participle of assortir ('to match, group by kind, stock with matching goods'), formed in Old/Middle French from a- (Latin ad-) + sorte ('kind, sort, category').

history.meaning: matched by kind or color, well-paired

atelier.etymology: Inherited from Old French astelier ('pile of wood chips; carpenter's yard or workshop'), derived from astele ('splinter, wood shaving, lath'), from Late Latin astella, diminutive of Classical Latin astula / assula ('splinter, chip of wood').

history.meaning: carpenter's woodyard -> craftsman's or artist's workshop

attacher.etymology: Inherited from Old French atachier ('to fasten, nail, tie'), altered by prefix substitution (a- for es-) from Old French estachier ('to fasten to a stake'), from Frankish *stakka ('stake, post, peg').

history.meaning: stake, peg -> to fasten to a peg, attach

atteindre.etymology: Inherited from Old French ateindre ('to touch upon, overtake, reach'), from Vulgar Latin *attingere for Classical Latin attingere ('to touch, reach, arrive at'), from ad- ('to') + tangere ('to touch').

history.meaning: to reach, attain, hit a mark

attendre.etymology: Attendre comes from Latin attendere, to direct one’s attention towards something. The eleventh-century French spelling was atendre; waiting and expecting developed around that idea of attention.

attention.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin attentionem (nominative attentio, 'mental application, attentiveness'), noun of action from attendere ('to stretch the mind toward, heed'), from ad- + tendere ('to stretch').

history.meaning: to direct the mind toward -> attentiveness

attraper.etymology: Formed in Old French (atraper, 12th c., 'to catch in a trap, ensnare') from a- (Latin ad-) + trape ('snare, trap', modern trappe), borrowed from Frankish *trappa ('trap, snare').

history.meaning: trap -> to catch in a trap
to catch, grab, get hold of

au.etymology: Au is the contraction of the preposition à and the masculine article le. It is a grammatical combination, not the unrelated chemical symbol Au. The Académie describes its use under à.

au-delà.etymology: Compound adverb and preposition formed from au ('at the', contraction of à + le) + delà ('on the other side, beyond', from Old French de la < Latin de illac 'from that side').

au-dessus.etymology: Compound adverb formed from au ('at the', à + le) + dessus ('on top, above', from Old French desus < de + sus < Latin sursum 'upward').

aube.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin alba ('dawn'), substantivized feminine of Classical Latin albus ('dull white'), elliptical for alba lux ('the white light on the horizon before sunrise').

history.meaning: first white light of morning, daybreak

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: aube (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: aube

aube.notes: Latin *al-* vocalized regularly to *au-* before consonants in Old French (*alba* -> **aube**, *alterum* -> **autre**, *calidum* -> **chaud**).

aucun.etymology: Inherited from Old French alcun ('some, someone, any'), from Vulgar Latin *aliqui-unus, altered from Classical Latin aliquis ('someone, anyone') + unus ('one'); through frequent use with negation ne, its sense shifted from positive ('some, any') to negative ('no, none').

history.meaning: any, some -> (with ne) no, not any, none

aujourd'hui.etymology: Univerbation of the Old/Middle French phrase au jour d'hui ('on the day of today'), where hui ('today', Old French ui) comes directly from Classical Latin hodie ('today' < hoc die 'on this day'); because hui was reduced to a single vowel, speakers reinforced it with au jour de ('on the day of').

history.meaning: literally 'on the day of today' -> today

aussi.etymology: Aussi developed from an older combination of al, meaning something else, and si, meaning thus. The Académie records twelfth-century alsi in a comparison expression; the modern adverb also acquired the sense too.

automne.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin autumnus ('autumn, harvest season'), a word of ancient Italic or Etruscan origin already opaque to Roman grammarians. The Latin -mn- spelling was restored in Middle French even though only /n/ is pronounced.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: automne (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: automne

automne.notes: The **-m-** is silent in **automne** (/otɔn/), resurging aloud in the adjective **automnal** (/otɔmnal/).

autour.etymology: Univerbation of the Old French phrase au tour ('in the turn or circuit of'), from au (à + le) + tour ('turn, circuit, circumference', deverbal from tourner).

history.meaning: in the circle of -> around, about

autre.etymology: Autre descends from Latin alter, the other of two. Tenth-century French distinguished masculine altre and feminine altra.

autrefois.etymology: Univerbation of Old French autre feiz / autre fois ('another time'), from autre ('other', Latin alter) + fois ('time, occasion', from Latin vicem 'turn, change').

history.meaning: at another time -> in former times, formerly

aux.etymology: Aux combines the preposition à with the plural article les. Like singular au, it belongs to the history of French preposition–article contractions rather than being an independent borrowed noun.

avaler.etymology: Avaler is derived from aval, downwards or downstream. Its eleventh-century intransitive sense was to descend; the swallowing sense developed as making something go down the throat.

avance.etymology: Avance is a noun built from avancer ('to move forward', from Vulgar Latin *abantiare, built on ab + ante 'from before').
avance.notes: **Être en avance** = to be early (ahead of schedule); **à l'avance** = beforehand.

avancer.etymology: Inherited from Old French avancier ('to move forward, promote'), from Vulgar Latin *abantiare, derived from Late Latin abante ('in front, before', source of avant).

avant.etymology: Inherited from Old French avant ('in front, forward, before'), from Late Latin abante ('in front of, before'), a compound preposition formed from ab ('from, off') + ante ('before, in front').

avec.etymology: Avec continues a reconstructed Popular Latin combination *apu(d)-hoc, approximately with this, strengthening apud, near or with. The early French forms avuec, avoc and avoec are recorded in the eleventh century.

avenue.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of Old/Middle French avenir ('to arrive, come up to', from Latin advenire 'to come to'); originally meant 'arrival, way of approach to a country house lined with trees', whence 'wide tree-lined thoroughfare'.

history.meaning: arrival, approach road to an estate

averse.etymology: Formed in early modern French by fusing the adverbial phrase à verse ('pouring down in buckets', as in il pleut à verse), built on verser ('to pour, tip over') from Latin versare.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: averse (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: averse

averse.notes: Compare **renverser** ('to spill or knock over') and **verser** ('to pour tea or soup'), both from the same root.

avis.etymology: Univerbation of the Old French phrase ce m'est a vis ('it seems to me', literally 'that is to me by way of view'), from à ('to, in') + vis ('sight, view, opinion', from Classical Latin visum, neuter past participle of videre 'to see').

history.form: visum -> a vis (in ce m'est a vis)

avoir.etymology: Avoir descends from Latin habere. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. Its central meaning concerns possession, and it also serves as an auxiliary in compound tenses.
avoir.notes:
- *Avoir* is used for age and many states: *avoir chaud, froid, faim, soif, peur, raison, tort*.
- *Il y a* means 'there is/are' and also 'ago': *il y a deux ans*.
- Along with *être*, it is one of the two auxiliary verbs of French.

axe.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin axis, axem ('axle, pivot, axis of the earth or sky'), from PIE *h2eks- ('axle').

history.meaning: geometric or mechanical axis, main line

aîné.etymology: Inherited from Old French ainsné ('firstborn, elder'), compound of ainz ('before, earlier', from Vulgar Latin *antius, comparative of ante 'before') + né ('born', from Latin natus).

aïe.etymology: Natural expressive exclamation of sudden sharp pain (attested since Old French aï / aïe), parallel to similar cries across Romance and European languages.

bagage.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from bague (in its older plural sense bagues 'bundles, packs, personal belongings', from Old Norse baggi 'pack, bundle' or a Gallo-Romance root) + collective suffix -age; Originally denoted an army's supply train before meaning a traveler's luggage.

bague.etymology: In the sense 'finger ring', borrowed in the 15th century from Old Occitan baga ('berry; metal ring or link'), from Classical Latin baca / bacca ('berry, pearl, link of a chain').

bail.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French baillier ('to hand over, entrust, administer'), inherited from Classical Latin bajulare ('to carry a burden, take charge of'), from bajulus ('porter, carrier').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French bail / baillif

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bail (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bail

bail.notes: Plural **baux** preserves the historical vocalization of *-l* before *-s* (**un bail**, **des baux**), and colloquially **ça fait un bail!** means 'it has been ages!'.

bain.etymology: Inherited from Old French bain ('bath, bathing place'), from Vulgar Latin *banneum, phonetic reduction of Classical Latin balneum / balineum ('bath'), borrowed from Ancient Greek balaneion ('bath, bathhouse').

baisser.etymology: Inherited from Old French baissier ('to lower, bring down'), from Vulgar Latin *bassiare ('to make low'), derived from Late Latin bassus ('low, short in stature').

balayer.etymology: Derived in Old French (baleiier, 12th c., 'to sweep with a broom') from balai ('broom, originally a bundle of broom twigs'), of Gaulish origin (*balatno- / *banatlo- 'broom plant, Genista', akin to Breton balan).

balcon.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian balcone ('projecting gallery or window platform'), itself derived from Lombardic *balko ('wooden beam, timber platform').

cognates.meaning: balcony via Italian; balk ('beam') from Old English balca

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: balcon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: balcon

balcon.notes: Renaissance Italian architecture brought **le balcon** into French cities, where wrought-iron railings later became a hallmark of classic facades.

banc.etymology: Inherited from Old French banc ('long wooden seat; market counter'), borrowed early from Frankish *bank ('bench, shelf').

cognates.meaning: bench is the native Germanic cousin; bank came via Italian banca
italianate relatives from the same Germanic root

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: banc (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: banc

banc.notes: The final *-c* in **un banc** **/bɑ̃/** is completely silent (just like **blanc** **/blɑ̃/** and **franc** **/fʁɑ̃/**).

bande.etymology: Represents two converged Germanic borrowings in Old French: (1) 'strip, band, ribbon', from Frankish *binda ('band, fillet', akin to English bind); and (2) 'troop, company of people', via Old Occitan banda from Gothic bandwa ('standard, banner around which a troop rallies').

history.meaning: strip of cloth; troop under a banner
strip, tape, border; band or group of people

barre.etymology: Inherited from Old French barre ('bar, barrier, rod'), from Vulgar Latin *barra ('crossbar, barrier'), probably of pre-Roman or Gaulish origin.

barreau.etymology: Formed in Old French (barel / barreau, 12th c.) as the diminutive of barre ('bar, rod') with suffix -el (> -eau); refers both to a window/cage bar and to the railing separating lawyers in court, hence the legal 'bar'.

history.meaning: small bar or railing; the legal bar

bas.etymology: Inherited from Old French bas ('low, not high'), from Late Latin bassus ('thickset, short, low in stature'), a word of Italic or Oscan origin originally used as a cognomen.

history.meaning: short, low, close to the ground

bassin.etymology: Inherited from Old French bacin ('wide bowl, water basin'), from Late/Medieval Latin baccinum ('water vessel'), widely traced to a Gaulish root *bacca ('trough, bowl').

history.meaning: fountain basin, garden pool, river basin

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bassin (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bassin

bassin.notes: In public French parks and squares, **le bassin** is the ornamental stone pool where fountains play and children sail toy boats.

battre.etymology: Inherited from Old French batre ('to strike, beat'), from Vulgar Latin *battere, reduced from Classical Latin batuere / battuere ('to beat, strike, fence'), possibly an ancient Gaulish borrowing in Latin.

beau.etymology: Beau continues Latin bellus, pretty or graceful. The eleventh-century French form bel survives as a modern alternative before certain vowel sounds.

beaucoup.etymology: Beaucoup joins beau, formerly able to mean large, and coup, a portion cut from a whole. The Académie records thirteenth-century biau cop with the sense of a large and fine thing.

bec.etymology: Inherited from Old French bec ('bird's bill, beak, spout'), from Classical Latin beccus ('beak'), explicitly recorded by Suetonius as a Gaulish word (*bekkos).

besoin.etymology: The Académie traces besoin probably to reconstructed Old Low Franconian *bisun(n)i, care or need. Thirteenth-century French had besoing. The proposed Germanic source is probable rather than certain.

beurre.etymology: Beurre comes from Latin butyrum, borrowed from Ancient Greek boútyron ('cow-cheese', from boûs 'cow' + tyrós 'cheese'), evolving through Old French burre into modern beurre.
beurre.notes: **Beurre doux** = unsalted butter; **beurre demi-sel / salé** = lightly salted / salted butter.

bibliothèque.etymology: Learned borrowing via Latin bibliotheca from Ancient Greek bibliothḗkē ('book repository, bookcase, library'), compounded from biblíon ('book, papyrus roll') and thḗkē ('case, chest, storage place', from tithénai 'to put').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bibliothèque (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bibliothèque

bibliothèque.notes: In French, **une bibliothèque** means both a public/private library AND a piece of furniture (a bookcase)—whereas **une librairie** is a bookshop.

bien.etymology: Bien descends from the Latin adverb bene, well. The Académie records it in French from the tenth century; the noun meaning a good or a possession developed from the adverb.

bientôt.etymology: Bientôt joins bien and tôt. Fourteenth-century bien tost meant in a short time, before the expression settled into its modern meaning soon.

bienvenue.etymology: Noun and adjective formed in Old French from bien ('well', from Latin bene) + venue, feminine past participle of venir ('to come', from Latin venire) — literally 'a good or happy arrival'.

billet.etymology: Formed in Middle French as a diminutive of bille ('short written note', an alteration of bulle 'sealed papal or official document', from Latin bulla 'leaden seal'); originally a short written note or pass, whence 'ticket' and 'banknote'.

history.meaning: short letter, written pass, ticket, banknote

biscuit.etymology: Compound inherited from Old French bescuit ('twice-baked bread'), modeled on Latin panis bis coctus: bis ('twice') + cuit (past participle of cuire 'to bake'). Originally it named dry, durable ship's bread baked a second time to drive out moisture.

history.meaning: crisp sweet cookie; light sponge cake

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: biscuit (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: biscuit

biscuit.notes: Ceramicists also call unglazed once-fired pottery **le biscuit** by analogy with dry baked biscuit.

bizarre.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian bizzarro ('irascible, touchy, capricious, strange', derived from bizza 'fit of anger'), originally meaning 'hot-tempered, valiant' in French before settling into 'odd, strange, eccentric' in the 17th century.

history.meaning: flash of anger -> fiery, capricious, strange

blanc.etymology: Blanc entered Gallo-Romance from Frankish *blank ('shining, gleaming white', cognate with English 'blank'), displacing Classical Latin albus in everyday speech.
blanc.notes: Feminine **blanche** preserves the palatalised final consonant: *une nappe blanche*.

bleu.etymology: Inherited from Old French bloe / bleu ('blue, pale, livid'), borrowed from Frankish *blao ('blue, gleaming', from Proto-Germanic *blewaz, cognate with English blue and German blau), which displaced Latin caeruleus in Western Romance.

bleui.etymology: Past participle of bleuir ('to turn blue, make blue'), formed in Old/Middle French from the adjective bleu ('blue') + verbal suffix -ir.

bloc.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century (originally losc / bloc) from Middle Dutch blok ('felled tree trunk, heavy mass of wood or stone'), from Proto-Germanic *bluka-.

history.meaning: heavy log, solid mass of wood or stone
solid lump or block; unified group, notepad

bloquer.etymology: Derived in the 15th century from bloc ('block, solid mass') or Middle Dutch blokken; originally a military verb meaning 'to hem in, blockade a fortress', later 'to jam, immobilize, block'.

history.meaning: to hem in, blockade -> to jam, immobilize, block

boire.etymology: Inherited from Old French boivre ('to drink'), from Classical Latin bibere ('to drink'), from PIE *pi-ph3-e- ('to drink').

bois.etymology: Bois descends from Medieval Latin boscus ('woodland, timber'), probably of Germanic origin (akin to English 'bush'). It means both a small forest ('woods') and the material 'wood'.
bois.notes: **En bois** = made of wood (e.g. *un train en bois*, *un escalier en bois*).

bol.etymology: In the sense 'hemispherical drinking or soup bowl', borrowed in the 17th–18th century from English bowl (Originally in punch bowl), from Old English bolla ('round vessel, bowl').

bon.etymology: Bon descends from Latin bonus, good. The Académie records tenth-century French buon; forms such as feminine bonne belong to this same adjective.

bonjour.etymology: Bonjour joins bon and jour. The Académie records thirteenth-century bon jor with the sense of a good day or happy time. The wish developed into the familiar daytime greeting.
bonjour.notes: Use bonjour to greet someone during the day. Saying it when taking leave is regional; au revoir is the general farewell. Bonsoir is the usual evening greeting.

bonsoir.etymology: Univerbation of the greeting phrase bon soir ('good evening'), from bon ('good', Latin bonus) + soir ('evening', from Latin serum, neuter of serus 'late').

bonté.etymology: Inherited from Old French bontet / bonté ('goodness, moral worth, kindness'), from Classical Latin bonitatem (nominative bonitas, 'goodness, kindness'), derived from bonus ('good').

bord.etymology: Inherited from Old French bort ('ship's side, edge, rim'), borrowed from Frankish *bord ('plank, side of a ship, edge', cognate with English board).

history.meaning: side of a ship; edge, shore, rim

border.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from bord ('edge, side of a ship') + verbal ending -er; means 'to edge, hem, line along the border' or 'to tuck in bedsheets'.

history.meaning: to line the edge of; to tuck in

bordure.etymology: Formed in Middle French from border ('to edge, border') or bord ('edge') + suffix -ure.

bouche.etymology: Inherited from Old French boche ('mouth'), from Classical Latin bucca ('puffed-out cheek; in informal and Vulgar Latin, mouth'), which completely replaced Classical Latin os, oris in Romance.

bouchée.etymology: Inherited from Old French bochiee ('a mouthful'), formed from bouche ('mouth') + suffix -ée denoting the quantity contained in something.

bouder.etymology: Attested since the 14th century ('to pout, sulk'), formed on an expressive root *bud- / *bod- évoquant puffed-out lips or a swollen belly (compare Old French boudine 'navel, paunch' and Provençal boudar 'to swell, pout').

bouger.etymology: Inherited from Old French bulgier / bougier ('to stir, bubble up, move'), from Vulgar Latin *bullicare ('to bubble, seethe, stir'), frequentative of Classical Latin bullire ('to boil, bubble').

bouillir.etymology: Inherited from Old French bolir / bouillir ('to boil, bubble'), from Classical Latin bullire ('to bubble, boil'), derived from bulla ('water bubble').

bouillon.etymology: Inherited from Old French boillon ('bubbling spring, boiling surge, broth'), derived from bouillir ('to boil') < Classical Latin bullire ('to bubble up'), itself from bulla ('water bubble').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from French bouillon and Old French boillir

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bouillon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bouillon

bouillon.notes: In 19th-century Paris, affordable neighborhood restaurants serving hot beef **bouillon** to workers gave rise to the classic Parisian **Bouillon** dining halls.

boulanger.etymology: Continued from Old Northern French / Picard boulenc (12th century) and boulengier, most plausibly traced by Bloch-Wartburg and the TLFi to Middle Dutch bolle ('round loaf of bread', related to boule). In medieval towns a boulanger baked round loaves, gradually displacing the older French word talmelier.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boulanger (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boulanger

boulangerie.etymology: Derived in Middle French from boulanger ('baker'), earlier Picard and Old French boulenc / boulengier ('maker of round loaves'), borrowed from Middle Dutch or Old Picard bolle ('round ball-shaped loaf').

history.meaning: round loaf -> baker of round loaves

cognates.meaning: round loaf of country bread; ball

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boulangerie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boulangerie

boulangerie.notes: Medieval French originally called a baker **talmelier** (from sifting flour); **boulanger** won out because customers prized plump round loaves.

boussole.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Italian bussola ('mariner's compass housed in a small boxwood case'), from Late Latin buxida ('little box made of boxwood'), altered from Greek pyxís (from pýxos 'box tree').

history.meaning: small box holding a magnetized needle

cognates.meaning: native inherited doublet from the same Late Latin buxida!
likewise ultimately from Late Latin buxus/buxis ('boxwood')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boussole (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boussole

boussole.notes: Astonishingly, **une boussole** ('compass') and **une boîte** ('box') are etymological twins — a compass was named after the little boxwood case protecting its needle!

bout.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (bot / bout, 'blow, thrust; extremity, end') from bouter ('to strike, push, thrust'), itself borrowed from Frankish *botan ('to strike, push, thrust', cognate with English butt).

history.meaning: to thrust -> end point, tip, small piece

bouteille.etymology: Inherited from Old French boteille ('bottle, flask'), from Late Latin butticula ('small cask or flask'), diminutive of buttis ('cask, wine-skin, barrel').

boutique.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Old Occitan botica ('shop, storehouse'), from Late Latin apotheca ('storehouse, wine-cellar, magazine'), itself from Ancient Greek apotheke ('repository, storehouse', from apotithenai 'to put away, store', the same Greek word that gave apothicaire and dépôt).

boîte.etymology: Inherited from Old French boiste ('small box, pyx'), from Vulgar Latin *buxida, borrowed from Late Greek pyxida (accusative of pyxis 'boxwood receptacle, small box'), derived from pyxos ('box tree, boxwood').

boîtier.etymology: Derived within French from boîte ('box') with the suffix -ier. Boîte itself goes back through Old French boiste to Late Latin buxida, from Greek pyxís ('small boxwood container', from pýxos 'box tree').

history.meaning: protective casing, watch case, junction box

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boîtier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boîtier

branche.etymology: Inherited from Old French branche ('tree bough, branch'), from Late Latin branca ('paw, claw of an animal'), which developed the metaphorical sense 'forking bough of a tree' in Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: animal paw or claw -> branching limb

brancher.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from branche ('branch'); originally meant 'to perch on a branch' (or hang a thief from a tree), then in modern technical usage 'to connect a branch pipe or electrical lead, plug in'.

history.meaning: to perch on a branch -> to tap a line, plug in, connect

bras.etymology: Inherited from Old French braz ('arm'), from Classical Latin bracchium ('forearm, arm'), borrowed from Ancient Greek brachion ('upper arm, arm').

bravo.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from Italian bravo! ('well done!, bold!, admirable!'), exclamation of the adjective bravo ('bold, wild, untamed'), probably from Vulgar Latin *bravus (an alteration of barbarus 'untamed, wild' or pravus 'crooked, fierce').

bricolage.etymology: Formed in Modern French from bricoler ('to do odd jobs, tinker; originally to rebound or zigzag', from Old/Middle French bricole 'catapult, rebound of a ball in court tennis', from Italian briccola) + suffix -age.

brillant.etymology: Present participle of briller ('to shine, sparkle') used as an adjective and noun (for a cut diamond) since the 17th century.

briller.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian brillare ('to sparkle, glitter'), likely derived from Vulgar Latin *beryllare ('to gleam like a beryl crystal'), from Latin beryllus < Greek beryllos ('beryl, sea-green gemstone').

history.meaning: beryl gem -> to sparkle like a gem

brin.etymology: Attested since the 16th century ('slender shoot of a plant, blade of grass, strand of thread, tiny bit'), of uncertain origin—probably a figurative use of Old French brin ('noise, clamor, dash') or from a pre-Latin/Celtic root *brinos ('rod, shoot').

history.meaning: slender plant shoot, blade, strand, tiny bit

brioche.etymology: Brioche appears in fifteenth-century Norman French, built on the dialect verb brier (Old French broier, 'to knead or pound dough with a wooden roller').
brioche.notes: **Une brioche à la cannelle** = a cinnamon roll/bun.

brique.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century via Picard/Flemish from Middle Dutch brike ('broken piece, flat cake, fired clay brick', related to breken 'to break').

cognates.meaning: borrowed in the 15th c. via French/Flemish
unrelated in form, whereas English break shares the Germanic root

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: brique (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: brique

brique.notes: In French culinary slang, rectangular milk or juice cartons are also called **des briques** (**une brique de lait**).

brise.etymology: Attested from the 16th century as a nautical term ('steady northeast wind, light breeze'), cognate with Spanish brisa and English breeze; of uncertain ultimate origin (possibly related to Old French bise 'cold north wind').

bristol.etymology: Shortened from papier bristol (early 19th century), named after the English port city of Bristol, whose paper mills became famous around 1800 for smooth, heavy pasted card stock (Bristol board).

history.meaning: fine calling card, index card, or recipe card

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bristol (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

bristol.notes: In France today, **une fiche bristol** (or simply **un bristol**) is every student's, librarian's, and baker's favorite sturdy index card.

bronze.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian bronzo ('copper-tin alloy, bell metal'), itself of debated origin—either from Medieval Latin aes Brundisinum ('copper of Brindisi, famous for bronze mirrors') or from Persian birinj ('copper, brass').

brouiller.etymology: Inherited from Old French broillier ('to dirty, mix up, confuse'), derived from broil / brouet ('broth, muddy mixture'), from a Gallo-Romance verb tied to Frankish *brod ('broth, brew', cognate with English broth).

history.meaning: broth, mixture -> to stir up, muddle, blur
to scramble, blur, jam, set at odds

bruit.etymology: Substantivized past participle of Old French bruire ('to roar, rumble, rustle'), from Vulgar Latin *brugere, a blend of Classical Latin rugire ('to roar') and fremere / bracare.

history.meaning: to roar, rumble -> noise, sound, rumor

brun.etymology: Inherited from Old French brun ('dark brown, dusky, gleaming'), borrowed from Frankish *brun ('brown, shining', from Proto-Germanic *brunaz, cognate with English brown).

bruyant.etymology: Adjective formed from the old present participle of bruire ('to roar, make noise', source of bruit).

bulle.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin bulla ('water bubble; round boss or amulet; leaden seal attached to papal documents').

history.meaning: papal bull; air or soap bubble, comic speech balloon

bureau.etymology: Inherited from Old French burel ('coarse woolen cloth'), derived from bure ('dark homespun wool cloth', from Late Latin burra 'shaggy wool'); shifted seamlessly from the coarse baize cloth covering a counting table -> the writing desk itself -> the office room -> the agency or staff working there.

history.meaning: coarse woolen cloth covering a counting-table
cloth-covered writing desk -> office room -> department

bus.etymology: Clipped in the 20th century from autobus ('motor bus'), itself modeled on omnibus (1828, from Latin omnibus 'for everyone', dative plural of omnis 'all').

buée.etymology: Derived from Old French buer ('to wash linen in steaming hot lye-ash water'), borrowed from Frankish *bukon ('to steep laundry in beech-ash lye'); the noun shifted from 'washhouse steam' to 'mist/condensation on cold glass'.

history.meaning: to soak linen in hot lye
vapor condensation on windows or glasses

cognates.meaning: to steep linen in hot lye

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: buée (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: buée

buée.notes: Unlike **vapeur** (steam rising in the air), **la buée** specifically names the fine mist that fogs a windowpane or a pair of spectacles.

cabinet.etymology: Formed in the 16th century (or reinforced by Italian gabinetto) as a diminutive of cabine ('small room, cabin'), denoting a small private room, study, closet, or professional office.

history.meaning: small private room, study, professional office, storage chest

cacher.etymology: Inherited from Old French cachier ('to press together, crush, tread down; later to conceal'), from Vulgar Latin *coacticare ('to press tightly together, stow away'), frequentative of Classical Latin coactare (from cogere 'to drive together, compress').

history.meaning: to press tightly together, pack away
to press down -> to tuck out of sight, hide

cadeau.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Occitan capdel ('capital letter heading a chapter', from Latin capitellum 'little head'); calligraphers' ornate flourished capitals became 'festive flourishes / treats offered to please someone', and by the 18th century 'a gift'.

cognates.meaning: native northern French doublet from capitellum

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cadeau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cadeau

cadeau.notes: Originally a calligrapher's decorative flourish added 'purely for pleasure rather than utility', **un cadeau** came to replace **un présent** in everyday French.

café.etymology: Café ultimately comes from Arabic qahwa through Turkish qahve. The Académie considers Italian caveé or caffè the probable intermediary into French. It records the seventeenth-century French spellings cauueh and cafeh.
café.notes:
- *Un café* in France is normally a small, strong espresso. For a milky coffee, ask for *un café crème* or *un café au lait*.
- The same word names both the drink and the place.

cahier.etymology: Cahier comes from Old French quayer, cayer, from Vulgar Latin *quaternium (Latin quaternio, 'gathering of four folded sheets', from quattuor 'four'). English 'quire' (of paper) comes from the exact same Old French word!
cahier.notes: Used for school exercise books and large bound ledgers.

caisse.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Old Occitan caissa ('wooden chest, box'), inherited from Classical Latin capsa ('cylindrical box for book rolls, chest, coffer', from capere 'to hold, contain', doublets with native French châsse).

history.meaning: packing crate, cash box, checkout counter, car body

caler.etymology: Combines two sources: (1) 'to wedge, prop up with a chock', derived from cale ('wooden wedge', from Middle High German kil / dialectal German Keil 'wedge'); and (2) 'to lower a sail; to stall or give up', borrowed via Occitan calar from Late Latin chalare < Ancient Greek chalan ('to slacken, let down').

history.meaning: to lower a sail; to wedge firmly in place
to wedge steady; (of an engine) to stall

calme.etymology: Calme entered Middle French via Italian calma ('stillness free of wind at sea'), ultimately from Late Latin cauma and Ancient Greek kaûma ('midday heat', when flocks and winds rest).
calme.notes: Both adjective (*une cour calme*) and masculine noun (*le calme*).

calmer.etymology: Derived in the 15th century from calme ('calm, windless stillness at sea'), borrowed via Italian calmo / calma from Late Latin cauma ('burning heat of the midday sun when the wind drops and all rests'), from Ancient Greek kauma ('burning heat', from kaiein 'to burn').

history.meaning: midday heat when winds die down -> stillness, calm
to make calm, soothe, quiet down

camion.etymology: Attested in the 14th century in northern French (Norman-Picard camion, originally 'very small pin' and later 'low heavy dray or cart'), of uncertain origin.

history.meaning: low heavy dray or wagon -> motor truck, lorry

camionnette.etymology: Formed in late nineteenth-century French as the diminutive (-ette) of camion ('heavy dray cart, truck'), originally a Norman-Picard dialect word (camion, 14th c.) for a low transport dray.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: camionnette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: camionnette

camomille.etymology: Borrowed via Medieval Latin camomilla from Ancient Greek khamaímēlon, literally 'ground-apple' (khamaí 'on the earth, low-growing' + mêlon 'apple'), because fresh chamomile blossoms give off a crisp scent of ripe apples.

cognates.meaning: chamomile (literally 'little apple', a calque of the Greek!)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: camomille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: camomille

camomille.notes: Spanish **manzanilla** ('little apple') translates the Greek metaphor directly into Romance.

cannelle.etymology: Cannelle comes from Old French canele ('little reed or tube', diminutive of canne from Latin canna 'reed'), named after the rolled quill shape of dried cinnamon bark.
cannelle.notes: Italian *cannella* and Spanish *canela* share the exact same image of a rolled reed.

capitaine.etymology: Inherited from Old/Middle French capitaine, from Late Latin capitaneus ('prominent in size, chief, leader'), formed on Classical Latin caput, capitis ('head').

history.meaning: leader of a company or vessel

cognates.meaning: both borrowed from Old French forms of capitaneus
native doublet directly from Latin caput

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: capitaine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: capitaine

capitaine.notes: **Chef** and **capitaine** both grow from Latin **caput** ('head'), one through popular Gallo-Romance sound change and the other through medieval administrative Latin.

capricieux.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century from Italian capriccioso ('whimsical, subject to sudden starts'), derived from capriccio ('sudden shudder or whim', from capo 'head' + riccio 'hedgehog, curled/standing on end' — originally 'a head with hair standing on end').

capsule.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin capsula ('small box or coffer'), diminutive of capsa ('cylindrical box for papyrus rolls'), related to capere ('to hold, contain').

history.meaning: small sealed container, seed pod, time capsule

cognates.meaning: crate / reliquary box (doublets from Latin capsa)
borrowed via French from Latin capsula

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: capsule (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: capsule

capsule.notes: In everyday French, **une capsule** can mean a bottle cap, a coffee pod, a space capsule, or **une capsule temporelle** ('time capsule').

car.etymology: Inherited from Old French quar / car ('for, because, therefore'), phonetic reduction of Classical Latin quare ('by what means, wherefore, why, therefore', literally qua re 'by which thing').

history.meaning: by which thing, wherefore, for which reason

carafe.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian caraffa ('glass water decanter'), from Arabic gharrafa ('drinking vessel, ladle, water-scoop'), derived from gharafa ('to draw or scoop up water').

history.meaning: vessel for scooping water -> glass decanter
flared glass water or wine pitcher

carnet.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Old Occitan carnet / quernet ('small group of four folded sheets of paper, booklet'), diminutive of quern ('quire of four sheets', French cahier), from Vulgar Latin *quaternum (from quattuor 'four').

history.meaning: gathering of four folded sheets -> small notebook
pocket notebook, booklet of tickets or checks

carotte.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Latin carota ('carrot'), itself from Ancient Greek karōtón, replacing the older medieval French name pastenade.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: carotte (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: carotte

carotte.notes: Notice the spelling contrast between French **carotte** (one *r*, two *t*'s) and English **carrot** (two *r*'s, one *t*).

carreau.etymology: Inherited from Old French quarrel ('four-sided block, square tile, crossbow bolt'), from Vulgar Latin quadrellum, diminutive of quadrum ('square', related to quattuor 'four'). From 'little square', it came to name both floor tiles and rectangular windowpanes.

history.meaning: tile; windowpane; check pattern; diamonds (in cards)

cognates.meaning: (archaic) square-headed crossbow bolt, from Old French quarrel

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: carreau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: carreau

carreau.notes: In everyday French, **faire les carreaux** means 'to wash the windows'.

carrière.etymology: In the career sense, carrière was borrowed from Old Provençal carriera, street, ultimately from a Latin expression for a road for carts. Its sixteenth-century French sense concerned a space for running horses. The quarry noun has a separate origin.

carré.etymology: Inherited from Old French quarré ('four-cornered, square'), from Classical Latin quadratus ('squared, four-sided'), past participle of quadrare ('to make square'), from quattuor ('four').

carte.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (replacing native Old French charte in everyday senses) from Classical Latin charta ('sheet of papyrus, paper, document'), from Ancient Greek chartes ('leaf of papyrus').

history.meaning: sheet of papyrus or stiff paper

cartographe.etymology: Modern scholarly compound formed from carte ('map', from Latin charta 'sheet of papyrus') + -graphe (from Ancient Greek gráphein 'to draw, write, chart').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cartographe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

cartographe.notes: Note that French **une carte** covers 'map', 'postcard' (**carte postale**), 'menu/wine list', and 'playing card' all in a single word.

cartographie.etymology: Learned compound coined in the early 19th century from carte ('map', from Latin charta) + -graphie (from Ancient Greek graphein 'to write, draw').

history.meaning: the art and science of drawing maps

carton.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian cartone ('heavy pasteboard, full-scale preparatory drawing for a fresco'), augmentative of carta ('paper', from Latin charta) with suffix -one.

history.meaning: thick paper, pasteboard; artist's full-scale sketch

cas.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin casus ('a falling, chance occurrence, event, grammatical case'), action noun from cadere ('to fall').

history.meaning: to fall -> a fall, chance event, circumstance

casser.etymology: Inherited from Old French quasser ('to shatter, break into pieces'), from Classical Latin quassare ('to shake violently, batter, shatter'), frequentative of quatere ('to shake').

catastrophe.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally by Rabelais for the final turning point or denouement of a tragedy) via Late Latin catastropha from Ancient Greek katastrophe ('an overturning, sudden turn, tragic conclusion'), from kata- ('down') + strephein ('to turn').

cause.etymology: Cause was borrowed from Latin causa, which could mean both a cause and a legal case. The Académie dates the French noun to the twelfth century.

cave.etymology: Cave comes from Latin cava ('hollow place, underground vault', feminine substantive of cavus 'hollow'). In French it denotes a cellar beneath a building (whereas an outdoor rock cave is une grotte).
cave.notes: False friend: **la cave** is a basement or wine cellar, not a wild mountainside cave (*une grotte*).

ce.etymology: Ce continues reconstructed Popular Latin *ecce hoc, a strengthened form of this. The tenth-century French form czo or ço weakened to ce when unstressed; c’ is its modern elided form.

ceci.etymology: Compound demonstrative pronoun formed in Old/Middle French (ce ci, 14th c.) from ce ('this, that', from Vulgar Latin *ecce hoc 'behold this') + adverbial particle ci ('here', from *ecce hic 'behold here').

cela.etymology: Compound demonstrative pronoun formed in Old/Middle French (ce la) from ce ('this, that', < Vulgar Latin *ecce hoc) + adverbial particle là ('there', < Latin illac 'that way, there').

celui.etymology: Celui and celle developed from strengthened Latin demonstrative forms, reconstructed as *ecce illui and *ecce illa(m). Tenth-century French had cels as an oblique masculine plural form.

celui-là.etymology: Compound demonstrative pronoun formed from celui ('that one, the one', from Old French cel + lui < Vulgar Latin *ecce illui) + deictic particle -là ('there').

history.meaning: that one over there, the former

cent.etymology: Cent descends from Latin centum, hundred. Its French use as a number is recorded from the tenth century; the unrelated monetary cent is a later borrowing from American English.

centime.etymology: Coined during the French Revolution (monetary law of 1795) from Latin centesimus ('hundredth', from centum 'hundred'), replacing earlier centième for the one-hundredth subdivision of the franc.

centimètre.etymology: Coined in 1793–1795 during the introduction of the metric system from combining form centi- ('hundredth', from Latin centum 'hundred') + mètre ('meter', from Greek metron 'measure').

centre.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin centrum ('stationary point of a pair of compasses, center of a circle'), from Ancient Greek kentron ('sharp point, goad, stationary pivot of a compass'), from kentein ('to prick').

history.meaning: compass spike, center of a circle

cercle.etymology: Inherited via Old French cercle from Classical Latin circulus ('circular figure, ring, orbit'), diminutive of circus ('ring, circular arena').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cercle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cercle

cercle.notes: In French pastry kitchens, **un cercle à tarte** is the bottomless metal pastry ring that gives bakery tarts crisp vertical edges.

certainement.etymology: Formed in Old French from the feminine adjective certaine ('certain, sure', from Vulgar Latin *certanus < Classical Latin certus) + adverbial suffix -ment.

cession.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin cessionem (nominative cessio, 'a giving up, surrendering, legal transfer of rights'), action noun from cedere ('to yield, give up').

history.meaning: to yield -> legal surrender or transfer of property

chacun.etymology: Inherited from Old French chascun ('each one, everyone'), from Vulgar Latin *cascunus, a blend of *cata unum (from Greek kata 'by, apiece' + Latin unum 'one') and Classical Latin quisque unus ('each single one').

chaise.etymology: Chaise originated as a fifteenth-century Parisian pronunciation variant of chaire (from Latin cathedra, Ancient Greek kathédra 'seat', where r and z swapped in speech). Chaire kept the elevated sense of 'pulpit, academic chair', while chaise became the everyday chair.

chaleur.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin calorem (accusative of calor, 'heat, warmth', from calere 'to be warm'). Regular Gallo-Romance palatalisation turned initial ca- before a into cha- (/ʃa/) and Latin -orem into French -eur.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chaleur (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chaleur

chaleur.notes: Latin abstract nouns in *-or* were masculine, which evolved into feminine nouns in French (**la chaleur**, **la couleur**, **la douleur**).

chaleureux.etymology: Derived in Middle French from chaleur ('heat, warmth', from Latin calorem) + adjectival suffix -eux (Latin -osus).

chambre.etymology: Chambre develops regularly from Latin camera ('vaulted ceiling, arched room', from Ancient Greek kamára). As k softened before a to ch and m-r developed a glide b, camera became Old French chambre ('room, bedroom').
chambre.notes: Chambre is specifically a bedroom or hotel room; a general room of a house or flat is **une pièce**.

chance.etymology: Inherited from Old French cheance ('the way the dice fall, luck, fortune'), from Vulgar Latin *cadentia ('a falling'), neuter plural of present participle cadens from Classical Latin cadere ('to fall').

history.meaning: fall of the dice -> luck, good fortune, opportunity

changement.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th c.) from changier / changer ('to change, exchange') + nominal suffix -ment.

history.meaning: act or result of changing, alteration

changer.etymology: Inherited from Old French changier ('to exchange, barter, alter'), from Late Latin cambiare ('to barter, exchange'), borrowed from Gaulish *kambion ('exchange, barter', from PIE *kemb- 'to bend, turn, change').

chanson.etymology: Inherited from Spoken Latin cantionem (accusative of cantio, 'singing, song, incantation', from canere / cantare 'to sing'). Before a, Latin c- shifted to ch- and -tio- became -son.

history.meaning: sung poem, song (as in chanson de geste)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chanson (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chanson

chantant.etymology: Adjective formed from the present participle of chanter ('to sing'); describes a voice, accent, or melody that has a musical, lilting cadence.

chanter.etymology: Inherited from Old French chanter ('to sing'), from Classical Latin cantare ('to sing, chant'), originally the frequentative of canere ('to sing').

chapeau.etymology: Inherited from Old French chapel ('wreath of flowers, hood, hat'), from Vulgar Latin cappellum, diminutive of Late Latin cappa ('hooded cloak, cape').

history.meaning: hooded cape -> little hood, head covering
garland or hat worn on the head

cognates.meaning: from Old French chapelet and Late Latin cappa

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chapeau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chapeau

chapeau.notes: Tipping one's hat in respect gave French the standalone exclamation **Chapeau!** ('Hats off! Well done!').

chaque.etymology: Detached in Middle French as a proclitic determiner from Old French chascun ('each one'), or directly continuing Old French chasque (from Vulgar Latin *cascus < *cata + quisque).

chariot.etymology: Formed in Old French with suffix -ot from charriier / char ('wheeled cart'), inherited from Gallo-Latin carrus ('four-wheeled Celtic wagon'), itself from Gaulish *karros.

history.meaning: trolley, book cart, luggage or pastry cart

cognates.meaning: all borrowed through Old/Anglo-Norman French from carrus

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chariot (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chariot

chariot.notes: Note that traditional French spells **chariot** with a single *-r-* (unlike **charrette** and **charrier**), though the 1990 spelling recommendations also allow *charriot*.

charmant.etymology: Present participle of charmer ('to cast a spell over, delight', from charme < Latin carmen 'ritual song, incantation, spell') used as an adjective since the 16th–17th century.

charnière.etymology: From Old French charniere ('hinge, pivot, joint'), formed on Spoken Latin *cardinaria from Classical Latin cardo, cardinis ('door pivot, hinge, axis'—the same Latin root that gave English cardinal, originally 'pivotal').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: charnière (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: charnière

charpente.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old/Middle French from charpenter ('to work timber, build framework', from Late Latin carpentare), derived from Classical Latin carpentum ('two-wheeled wooden carriage'), borrowed from Gaulish *karbanton ('wagon, chariot').

chasseur.etymology: Inherited from Old French chaceor ('hunter, huntsman'), agent noun formed from chacier / chasser ('to hunt, chase', from Vulgar Latin *captiare, frequentative of capere 'to catch') + suffix -eur.

history.meaning: to try to catch, hunt -> hunter
hunter; light infantry soldier, hotel bellhop

chaud.etymology: Chaud comes from Latin calidus (syncopated in spoken Latin to caldus, 'warm, hot'): initial ca- became cha- and l before d vocalised to u, giving Old French chalt, chaud.

chaudière.etymology: Inherited from Old French chaudiere ('large cooking cauldron, kettle'), from Late Latin caldaria ('vessel for hot water, warm bath-house'), derived from caldus / calidus ('hot, warm').

history.meaning: large cauldron -> steam or central-heating boiler

chauffage.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from chauffer ('to heat, warm') + suffix -age; originally meant 'firewood supply or right to gather firewood', then 'heating of a building'.

history.meaning: fuel supply -> system or act of heating

chauffer.etymology: Inherited from Old French chaufer ('to warm, heat'), from Vulgar Latin *calefare, reduced from Classical Latin calefacere ('to make warm or hot'), compound of calere ('to be warm') + facere ('to make').

chaufferie.etymology: Formed in Modern French from chauffer ('to heat, stoke a furnace') + suffix -erie denoting a workplace or installation.

chauffeur.etymology: Derived from chauffer ('to heat, stoke') + agent suffix -eur; originally denoted the fireman or stoker who tended a steam engine, and was transferred around 1895 to the driver of the earliest steam- and petrol-powered automobiles.

history.meaning: stoker of a furnace or steam engine

chausser.etymology: Inherited from Old French chaucier ('to put on shoes or hose'), from Classical Latin calceare ('to furnish with shoes, put on shoes'), derived from calceus ('shoe, half-boot', from calx, calcis 'heel').

history.meaning: to put on or fit with footwear

chaussure.etymology: Chaussure derives from Old French chauceüre, built on chausser ('to put on shoes or hose'), ultimately from Latin calceare and calceus ('shoe', from calx 'heel').
chaussure.notes: Paired with **chausser** (*chausser du 40* = to wear size 40 shoes).

cheffe.etymology: Feminine form of chef ('head, leader, chief cook', attested in Swiss and French usage since the 19th–20th century), ultimately from Old French chief ('head, leader') < Classical Latin caput ('head').

history.meaning: female head, director, or head chef

chemin.etymology: Inherited from Old French chemin ('way, road, path'), from Vulgar Latin *camminus, borrowed from Gaulish *kamminos ('way, path', derived from the Celtic root *kamm- / *keng- 'step, stride', cognate with Old Irish céimm and Welsh cam 'step').

chemise.etymology: Inherited from Old French chemise ('linen undershirt or shift'), from Late Latin camisia ('linen nightgown or soldier's tunic', recorded by St. Jerome in the 4th c.), borrowed via Germanic or directly from Gaulish *camisia.

cher.etymology: Cher comes from Latin carus, which already had both the senses beloved and costly. The Académie records the French adjective from the tenth century.

chercher.etymology: Chercher descends from Late Latin circare ('to go around, patrol, search everywhere', from circus 'circle'). Old French cerchier gave English 'search' while assimilating in French to chercher.
chercher.notes: No preposition for 'for': **chercher ses clés** = 'to look for one's keys'.

chevet.etymology: Inherited from Old French chevez ('bolster, head of a bed'), from Vulgar Latin *capicium (or Classical Latin capitium 'neck-opening of a tunic, head-end'), derived from caput ('head').

history.meaning: head -> part around or under the head
head of a bed, bedside; apse end of a church

cheville.etymology: Inherited via Old French cheville ('wooden peg, pin') from Vulgar Latin clavicula ('little key, peg, bolt'), diminutive of Classical Latin clavis ('key'). Because the anklebone juts out on either side of the foot like a rounded wooden peg, cheville became the standard French word for 'ankle'.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cheville (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cheville

cheville.notes: Luthiers still call violin and guitar tuning pegs **les chevilles**.

chez.etymology: Inherited from Old French chies / chez ('at the house of'), unstressed proclitic development of Classical Latin casa ('hut, cottage; in Vulgar Latin, house, home', originally in the ablative/locative phrase in casa 'in the house of').

history.meaning: hut, cottage -> in the house of
at the home, shop, or country of

chiffon.etymology: Formed in the 17th century as a diminutive of chiffe ('scrap of flimsy cloth, rag'), itself of uncertain origin (possibly an expressive form or related to Old French chipe 'rag', akin to English chip).

history.meaning: scrap of cloth, rag; sheer fabric

chiffre.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French (cifre, 13th c., originally 'the figure zero', then 'any Arabic numeral or secret code') via Medieval Latin cifra from Arabic sifr ('empty, zero', a calque of Sanskrit sunya 'void, zero').

history.meaning: zero -> numerical digit, total sum, cipher code

choc.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 16th century from choquer ('to strike against, collide, shock'), borrowed from Middle Dutch schocken ('to jolt, collide, strike together').

history.meaning: to jolt, collide -> violent impact, shock
