choisir.etymology: Inherited from Old French choisir ('to catch sight of, perceive clearly, pick out'), borrowed from Frankish *kausjan ('to taste, test, examine, choose', from Proto-Germanic *kausijana, causative of *keusana, cognate with English choose).

history.meaning: to spot, discern -> to choose, select

choix.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (chois, 12th c.) from choisir ('to discern, select, choose').

history.meaning: act or power of choosing, choice

chose.etymology: Chose descends from Latin causa. In later everyday Latin, the word expanded from cause or case to the broad meaning thing, replacing uses of res. The French form is recorded from the ninth century.

chuchoter.etymology: Expressive verb attested since the 16th century (earlier chucheter), formed on the hushed onomatopoeia chut / chu-chu imitating soft sibilant whispering.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chuchoter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chuchoter

chuchoter.notes: Say **chuchoter** **/ʃyʃɔte/** aloud and its two */ʃ/* sounds literally sound like two people whispering in a quiet library!

chêne.etymology: Inherited from Old French chaisne / chesne ('oak tree'), from Vulgar Latin *cassanus, metathesized from Gaulish *cassanos ('oak', literally 'gnarled or twisted tree').

ciel.etymology: Inherited from Old French ciel ('sky, heaven'), from Classical Latin caelum ('sky, vault of heaven').

cinq.etymology: Inherited from Old French cinc ('five'), from Vulgar Latin *cinque, dissimilated from Classical Latin quinque ('five', from PIE *penkwe).

cinquante.etymology: Inherited from Old French cinquante ('fifty'), from Vulgar Latin *cinquanta, dissimilated and contracted from Classical Latin quinquaginta ('fifty').

circulation.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin circulationem (nominative circulatio, 'a circular course or revolution'), derived from circulari ('to form a circle, move in a circle'); applied to blood in the 17th century and to street traffic in the 19th century.

history.meaning: blood flow, currency flow, street traffic

circuler.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin circulari ('to form a circle, gather in groups to talk, move around'), derived from circulus ('little circle, ring').

history.meaning: circle -> to move around in a circuit
to flow in a circuit, move about, travel

cire.etymology: Inherited via Old French cire from Classical Latin cera ('beeswax, wax writing tablet, wax seal'), cognate with Ancient Greek kērós ('beeswax').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cire

cire.notes: Rubbing linen with melted **cire** to waterproof it gave French **la toile cirée** ('oilcloth / waxed cloth') and the fisherman's yellow **ciré** raincoat.

cirer.etymology: Derived in Old French (cirer, 12th c., 'to coat or rub with wax') from cire ('beeswax', from Classical Latin cera 'wax').

history.meaning: wax -> to wax, polish shoes or floors

citron.etymology: Citron derives from Latin citrus ('citron tree'), extended with -on in French to name the yellow lemon (whereas English 'citron' kept the older sense of a thick-rind citrus fruit).
citron.notes: False friend in reverse: French **citron** is an everyday yellow lemon; a green lime is **un citron vert**.

citronnier.etymology: Formed within French from citron ('lemon', from Latin citrum) plus the productive tree-naming suffix -ier (from Latin -arius).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: citronnier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: citronnier

clair.etymology: Inherited from Old French cler ('bright, shining, clear-sounding, evident'), from Classical Latin clarus ('loud, clear-sounding; bright, shining, distinct, famous').

clairement.etymology: Formed in Old French (clerement) from the feminine adjective clere / claire ('clear, bright') + adverbial suffix -ment.

clic.etymology: Onomatopoeic noun (attested from the 16th–18th century) imitating the short sharp metallic sound of a latch, trigger, or switch; reinforced in the late 20th century by English click (computer mouse click).

client.etymology: Client was borrowed from Latin cliens, clientis ('follower under a patron's protection'), expanding in modern French to mean a customer, hotel guest, or professional client.
client.notes: In a hotel, **un client / une cliente** means a hotel guest.

clignoter.etymology: Frequentative verb formed in Middle French from cligner ('to blink, wink, half-close the eyes') with the iterative suffix -oter ('to do repeatedly in small bursts'). Cligner descends from Spoken Latin *cliniare, related to clinare ('to incline, lower').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: clignoter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: clignoter

cloche.etymology: Cloche comes from Medieval Latin clocca ('bell'), a word spread across Europe by early Irish missionary monks (Old Irish cloc 'bell', ultimately imitative of ringing). English 'clock' comes from the exact same root!
cloche.notes: Diminutive **la clochette** = small handbell or gate bell.

clocher.etymology: Inherited from Old French clochier ('bell tower, steeple'), derived from cloche ('bell', from Late Latin clocca, brought across Europe by Early Medieval Irish missionaries, cf. Old Irish clocc 'bell') + place suffix -ier.

clochette.etymology: Diminutive in -ette of cloche ('bell'), from Merovingian/Medieval Latin clocca ('handbell'), spread across Western Europe by early Irish missionary monks (compare Old Irish cloc 'bell').

cognates.meaning: originally a bell-striking timepiece, from the same clocca word

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: clochette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: clochette

clochette.notes: Because early mechanical tower clocks had no dials and announced hours purely by ringing a bell, Medieval Latin **clocca** gave French **cloche** ('bell') and English **clock**.

cloison.etymology: Inherited from Old French cloison ('enclosure, fence, partition wall'), from Vulgar Latin *clausionem, derived from claudere (past participle clausus, 'to close, shut off').

clé.etymology: Clé (also spelled clef) comes from Latin clavis ('key, bolt'), related to claudere ('to close'). Final v dropped in spoken French while spelling preserved -f in clef until modern clé became standard.
clé.notes: **Fermer à clé** = to lock; **sous clé** = under lock and key.

clôture.etymology: Inherited via Old French closture from Late Latin claustura ('barrier, enclosure, fastening'), formed on claudere, clausum ('to shut, close').

cognates.meaning: from sister formations on Latin claudere

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: clôture (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: clôture

clôture.notes: Once again, the circumflex in **clôture** preserves the memory of the vanished *-s-* in Old French **closture**.

coffre.etymology: Inherited from Old French cofre ('strongbox, chest'), from Classical Latin cophinus ('wicker basket'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kophinos ('large basket'), with consonantal change -phn- > -fr- (doublet of couffin).

cogner.etymology: Inherited from Old French coignier ('to drive in a wedge, stamp coins with a die, strike hard'), from Classical Latin cuneare ('to wedge, force with a wedge'), derived from cuneus ('wedge', source of French coin).

history.meaning: to drive a wedge -> to knock, bang, bump against

coin.etymology: Inherited from Old French coin ('iron wedge; minting die; angle, corner'), from Classical Latin cuneus ('wedge; wedge-shaped block or corner').

coincer.etymology: Derived in the 17th century from coin ('wedge, corner'); originally a carpenter's and printer's term meaning 'to secure tightly with wedges', then 'to jam, trap in a corner'.

history.meaning: to wedge tight -> to jam, get stuck, corner

collant.etymology: Present participle of coller ('to glue, stick, cling closely'); used as an adjective ('sticky, skin-tight') and since the 20th century as a noun for tights or pantyhose.

colle.etymology: Inherited from Old French cole ('paste, glue'), from Late Latin colla, borrowed from Ancient Greek kolla ('glue, paste made from hides or fish').

coller.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from colle ('glue, paste') + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: to glue, paste, stick or press closely against

colline.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian collina ('gentle hill'), derived from Classical Latin collis ('hill', adjective collinus 'of a hill').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: colline (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: colline

colline.notes: Lyon is traditionally described through its two famous **collines**: Fourvière (*la colline qui prie*) and la Croix-Rousse (*la colline qui travaille*).

colonne.etymology: Inherited from Old French colombe / colone ('pillar, column'), from Classical Latin columna ('pillar, post, column', related to columen 'summit, gable, prop').

history.meaning: architectural pillar, vertical column of text or troops

colère.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin cholera ('biliousness, choler, one of the four bodily humors in ancient medicine'), from Ancient Greek kholera / khole ('bile, gall, anger').

history.meaning: bilious humor believed to cause hot temper

combien.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (com bien, 12th c.) of com ('how, as', from Vulgar Latin *quomo < Classical Latin quomodo 'in what manner') + bien ('well, much', from Latin bene).

commande.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (comande, 'entrusted deposit; order, command') from comander / commander.

commandement.etymology: Derived in Old French (comandement, 11th c.) from comander / commander ('to order, command') + nominal suffix -ment.

commander.etymology: Inherited from Old French comander ('to entrust to someone's care; to order, rule'), from Late Latin *commandare, altered from Classical Latin commendare ('to commit to one's charge, entrust') under the influence of mandare ('to order').

history.meaning: to entrust -> to give orders, command
to command, control; to order goods

comme.etymology: Comme developed from Latin quomodo, in what way, through later quomo. Early French had cum and com; com remained in use into the sixteenth century.

commencer.etymology: Inherited from Old French comencier ('to begin'), from Vulgar Latin *cominitiare ('to initiate, enter upon'), formed from com- ('with, intensive') + initiare ('to begin, initiate', from initium 'beginning').

comment.etymology: Inherited from Old French coment ('in what way, how'), formed from com ('how, as', from Vulgar Latin *quomo < Classical Latin quomodo) + the adverbial suffix -ment.

commercial.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from English commercial (itself formed on Latin commercium 'trade, commerce', from com- + merx, mercis 'merchandise'), or formed directly on French commerce + -ial.

complet.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin completus ('filled up, full, complete'), past participle of complere ('to fill up to the brim, fulfill'), from com- + plere ('to fill').

complimenter.etymology: Formed in the 17th century from compliment ('courteous expression of praise or respect', borrowed via Italian complimento and Spanish cumplimiento from Latin complere 'to fulfill what courtesy requires') + verbal suffix -er.

compliqué.etymology: Past participle of compliquer ('to fold together, entangle, make complex'), borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin complicare ('to fold or roll up together'), from com- ('together') + plicare ('to fold').

complètement.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the feminine adjective complète ('complete, full') + adverbial suffix -ment.

composer.etymology: Formed in Old French (composer, 12th c.) from com- ('together') + poser ('to place, set down', which came from Late Latin pausare 'to pause, rest' but took over the meanings of Classical Latin ponere, positum 'to put, place' and componere 'to put together').

compositrice.etymology: Feminine counterpart of compositeur ('one who puts together; musical composer'), borrowed from Latin compositor (from componere, compositum 'to put together, compose').

comprendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French comprendre ('to embrace, include, grasp with the mind'), from Classical Latin comprehendere ('to take hold of together, encompass, perceive'), from com- ('together') + prehendere ('to seize, grasp').

compte.etymology: Inherited from Old French conte ('calculation, tally, narrative'), from Classical Latin computus ('a calculation, reckoning'), derived from computare ('to count, sum up', from com- + putare 'to reckon'); respelled compte with etymological p in Middle French to distinguish financial reckoning from conte ('story').

compter.etymology: Compter comes from Latin computare, to calculate. French originally wrote conter; an etymological spelling with p became associated with counting, while conter retained the storytelling sense.

comptoir.etymology: From Old French comptoir / conteoir ('counting room, counting table'), formed on compter ('to count, reckon', from Latin computare) + the place/instrument suffix -oir (Latin -atorium). Originally the merchant's table where coins were tallied.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: comptoir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: comptoir

concert.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian concerto ('agreement, harmony of voices or instruments'), deverbal noun from concertare ('to contend, strive together; to bring into harmony, arrange together'), from Latin concertare.

conclure.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin concludere ('to shut up closely, enclose; to bring an argument to a close, infer'), from com- ('together, completely') + claudere ('to shut, close').

history.meaning: to shut up, bring to a close
to bring to an end, settle a deal, infer

condition.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin condicionem (nominative condicio, 'agreement, stipulation, terms, social rank or state'), from condicere ('to talk over together, agree upon'), from com- + dicere ('to say, appoint').

history.meaning: to agree upon -> stipulation, state, rank

confiance.etymology: Confiance was borrowed from Latin confidentia, trust, related to confidere. The Académie records thirteenth-century confience.

confiture.etymology: Derived in Old French (confiture, 13th c., 'prepared medicinal preserve, candied fruit') from confire ('to prepare, preserve fruit in sugar or honey', from Latin conficere, confectum 'to prepare thoroughly').

history.meaning: to prepare, preserve in sugar -> fruit jam or preserve

confusion.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin confusionem (nominative confusio, 'a pouring or mingling together, disorder, blushing shame'), from confundere ('to pour together, mix up, throw into disorder').

history.meaning: to pour together -> mingling, disorder, embarrassment

connaître.etymology: Inherited from Old French conoistre ('to know, recognize, be acquainted with'), from Classical Latin cognoscere ('to become acquainted with, learn, know'), formed from co- ('with') + gnoscere / noscere ('to come to know').

consigne.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 16th century from consigner ('to seal, deposit in custody, give formal orders to a sentry', from Latin consignare 'to seal, register, attest'); denotes both strict standing orders and a baggage checkroom or bottle deposit.

history.meaning: to register under seal -> sentry's orders, instructions; left-luggage office

content.etymology: Content comes from Latin contentus, satisfied, the past participle of continere, to contain or hold within. The French adjective is recorded from the thirteenth century.

continu.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin continuus ('joining together, uninterrupted, successive'), derived from continere ('to hold together', from com- + tenere).

continuer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin continuare ('to join together in an unbroken series, carry on without interruption'), derived from continuus ('uninterrupted').

history.meaning: unbroken -> to carry on without break

contrat.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (originally contract) from Classical Latin contractus ('a drawing together; a business agreement or bargain'), action noun from contrahere ('to draw together, conclude a bargain').

contre.etymology: Inherited from Old French contre ('against, facing'), from Classical Latin contra ('against, opposite to, facing'), originally an instrumental/ablative feminine form built on com- ('with, together') with contrastive suffix *-trād.

history.meaning: against, close up against, in exchange for

contrôle.etymology: Contracted from Old and Middle French contrerolle ('duplicate parchment roll kept to verify an original tax or accounting register'), compound of contre ('against, alongside') + rôle ('scroll, roll' < Latin rotulus).

history.meaning: verification, inspection; later also 'mastery' via English

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: contrôle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: contrôle

contrôle.notes: This origin explains a classic French-English false friend: **un contrôle** in French usually means a 'check, inspection, or ticket check' (**liste de contrôle** = checklist), not domination.

conversation.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin conversationem (nominative conversatio, 'frequent abode in a place, intercourse, way of life, company'), from conversari ('to live with, keep company with'); narrowed in the 16th–17th century to 'familiar talk, conversation'.

history.meaning: social company -> exchange of spoken words

copeau.etymology: Inherited from Old French copel / coupeau ('wood chip, splinter shaved off with a blade'), derived from coper / couper ('to cut, strike off', from coup 'blow').

history.meaning: chip or shaving cut from wood
wood shaving, curl of planed wood or metal

corail.etymology: Inherited via Old French coral / corail from Classical Latin corallium, borrowed from Ancient Greek korállion ('red Mediterranean coral').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: corail (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: corail

corail.notes: When used as a noun for reef coral, the plural is **des coraux**, whereas as a color modifier (**des lentilles corail**, 'red lentils') **corail** stays invariable.

corde.etymology: Inherited from Latin chorda ('catgut string of a lyre or harp, cord'), borrowed from Ancient Greek khordḗ ('gut string of a musical instrument'). The musical sense is actually the oldest meaning of the word, older than 'rope'!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: corde (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: corde

corde.notes: From Latin *accordare* (originally debated between *cor* 'heart' and *chorda* 'tuning strings together') comes **accorder un piano**.

coton.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (via Italian cotone during Mediterranean trade) from Arabic quṭn / quṭun ('cotton').

cognates.meaning: borrowed directly from Andalusi Arabic al-quṭún (keeping article al-)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: coton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: coton

coton.notes: Compare French **coton** (via Italian, without the Arabic article) and Spanish **algodón** (which kept Arabic **al-** 'the').

couche.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (couche, 12th c., 'bed, resting place') from couchier / coucher ('to lay down, lie down', from Classical Latin collocare 'to place together, lay in bed'); extended to a stratum or layer laid flat, a coat of paint, and a baby's diaper.

history.meaning: to lay down -> bed, layer, coat, diaper

coucou.etymology: Onomatopoeic word attested since Old French (cucu / coucou), directly imitating the two-note spring call of the European cuckoo (Cuculus canorus), and used playfully as a peek-a-boo greeting ('peekaboo!, hi there!').

couler.etymology: Inherited from Old French coler ('to strain through a sieve, trickle, flow'), from Classical Latin colare ('to strain, filter a liquid'), derived from colum ('strainer, colander').

history.meaning: to trickle, flow, run; to cast metal; to sink

couleur.etymology: Inherited from Old French color / couleur ('color, hue, complexion'), from Classical Latin colorem (nominative color, 'hue, tint, complexion').

couloir.etymology: Formed from couler ('to flow, glide through', from Latin colare 'to strain, filter, flow') + -oir. Originally a strainer or narrow channel for liquids, by the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries un couloir came to mean a narrow indoor passageway through which people move from room to room.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: couloir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: couloir

coup.etymology: Inherited from Old French colp ('blow, strike'), from Vulgar Latin *colpus, synced from Late Latin colaphus ('a blow with the fist, buffet, cuff'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kolaphos ('buffet, slap').

history.meaning: blow, stroke, sudden action, drink, shot

coupe-papier.etymology: Compound noun formed in the 19th century from the verb stem coupe- (from couper 'to cut') + papier ('paper') — literally 'paper-cutter'.

history.meaning: blade for slitting uncut book pages or envelopes, letter opener

couper.etymology: Couper is derived from coup, a blow. Its early literal sense was dividing something with a blow; the verb is recorded from the eleventh century.

couple.etymology: Inherited from Old French cople ('leash tying two hounds together; pair, married or loving twosome'), from Classical Latin copula ('band, tie, bond, link', from co- + apere 'to fasten').

history.meaning: pair of animals or things (fem.); pair of partners (masc.)

cour.etymology: Cour descends from Popular Latin *curtis (from Classical Latin cohors, cohortis, 'enclosed yard, farmyard, retinue'). It denoted both an enclosed courtyard and a ruler's court; the dropped final t was never restored in spelling (unlike court 'short' from curtus).
cour.notes: **Donner sur la cour** = to overlook the courtyard (prized in French apartments and hotels for quiet).

courage.etymology: Inherited from Old French corage ('heart as the seat of feelings, inner spirit, valor'), from Vulgar Latin *coraticum, derived from Classical Latin cor, cordis ('heart') + suffix -aticum (> -age).

history.meaning: that which belongs to the heart, inner spirit

courir.etymology: Inherited from Old French corre / courir ('to run'), from Classical Latin currere ('to run, hasten'), shifted from the Latin 3rd conjugation to the French -ir class.

courrier.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Old Occitan corrier or Italian corriere ('mounted messenger who rides posthaste'), derived from Latin currere ('to run'); transferred from the messenger to the mail he carries.

cours.etymology: Cours descends from Latin cursus, the action of running. Its extended senses include a course or sequence of study. This is distinct from the later specialised noun for a broad avenue.

course.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Italian corsa ('act of running, race, raid at sea'), feminine participial noun from correre (< Latin currere, cursum 'to run'), replacing or supplementing older French cours.

court.etymology: Inherited from Old French cort ('short, brief'), from Classical Latin curtus ('clipped, docked, mutilated, short', from PIE *(s)ker- 'to cut').

cousin.etymology: Inherited from Old French cosin ('cousin, kinsman'), from Vulgar Latin *cosinus, contracted in rapid kinship address from Classical Latin consobrinus ('mother's sister's child, first cousin', from com- + sobrinus < soror 'sister').

coussin.etymology: Inherited from Old French coissin / coussin, from Vulgar Latin *coxinum ('seat pad for the hips'), derived from Classical Latin coxa ('hip', which itself evolved into French cuisse 'thigh').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: coussin (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: coussin

coussin.notes: Contrast **un coussin** (seat or sofa cushion) with **un oreiller** (bed pillow, from *oreille* 'ear').

cousu.etymology: Inherited from Old French cosu ('sewn, stitched'), past participle of coudre ('to sew'), from Vulgar Latin *cosere < Classical Latin consuere ('to sew together', from com- + suere 'to sew').

couvercle.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin cooperculum ('cover, lid'), an instrument noun built on cooperire ('to cover completely'—the same verb that gave French couvrir and English cover).

history.meaning: lid of a vessel or chest

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: couvercle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: couvercle

couverture.etymology: Inherited from Old French coverture ('covering, roof, bed-cover, dissimulation'), from Late/Vulgar Latin *cooperitura, formed on Classical Latin cooperire, coopertum ('to cover completely', source of couvrir).

history.meaning: roofing, bed blanket, book cover, insurance or media coverage

coéquipier.etymology: Formed in 20th-century French from prefix co- ('with, fellow') + équipier ('team member', from équipe 'team, crew').

coûter.etymology: Inherited from Old French coster ('to cost, require an outlay of money or effort'), from Classical Latin constare ('to stand together, stand firm; in commerce, to stand at a price, cost'), from com- + stare ('to stand').

history.meaning: to stand at a price, cost

craie.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin creta ('chalk, fine white clay, fuller's earth'). Regular loss of intervocalic -t- and diphthongisation of long ē turned creta into Old French creie, then craie.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: craie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: craie

craie.notes: English **crayon** was borrowed from French *crayon*, originally 'a small stick of **craie** (chalk)'.

cravate.etymology: Adopted in the mid-17th century as a phonetic adaptation of Croate ('Croatian'), naming the knotted linen neck-scarves worn by Croatian light horsemen serving in King Louis XIII and Louis XIV's Royal-Cravates regiment.

history.meaning: scarf knotted around the collar; necktie

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cravate (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cravate

cravate.notes: Croatia celebrates International Cravat Day every October in honor of how **la cravate** traveled from Croatian riders through Paris to wardrobes worldwide.

crayon.etymology: Crayon was formed in French from craie ('chalk', from Latin creta) + -on, originally meaning a piece of drawing chalk before naming the graphite pencil.
crayon.notes: False friend: **un crayon** is an ordinary pencil (*écrire au crayon* = 'write in pencil').

creux.etymology: Inherited from Old French crues ('hollow, empty inside, deep'), from Vulgar Latin *crosus ('hollowed out'), a pre-Romance (likely Gaulish or Celtic) word also found in Old Occitan cros ('hollow, hole').

crier.etymology: Inherited from Old French crier ('to proclaim publicly, shout, cry out'), from Vulgar Latin *critare, reduced from Classical Latin quiritare ('to raise a public outcry, appeal for help to the Quirites or Roman citizens').

history.meaning: to call on fellow citizens for help, cry aloud

crise.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century as a medical term ('decisive turning point of an illness') via Medieval Latin crisis from Ancient Greek krisis ('separation, decision, turning point of a disease'), from krinein ('to separate, decide, judge').

history.meaning: decisive judgment or turning point of a disease
medical turning point -> acute attack, social or economic crisis

crochet.etymology: Diminutive formed in Old French from croc ('hook, curved fang') + -et, with croc borrowed from Frankish *krōk or Old Norse krókr ('hook').

cognates.meaning: hooked needlework (from French); curved staff (from Norse)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: crochet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: crochet

crochet.notes: English borrowed **crochet** directly from French because the yarn is worked with a small hooked needle.

croire.etymology: Inherited from Old French creire ('to trust, have faith in, believe'), from Classical Latin credere ('to entrust, trust, believe', from archaic PIE compound *kred-dhe- 'to place one's heart or sacred trust').

croiser.etymology: Derived in Old French (croisier, 12th c., originally 'to take the Crusader's cross, mark with a cross, lay crosswise') from croiz / croix ('cross', from Classical Latin crucem).

history.meaning: cross -> to lay crosswise, take the cross
to cross, fold across, pass by each other, interbreed

croquis.etymology: Derived in the mid-18th century from the verb croquer ('to crunch', and figuratively among 17th-century painters 'to dash off or capture a subject briskly in a few strokes'), with suffix -is.

morphemes.meaning: result of an action (compare gâchis, fouillis)

cognates.meaning: borrowed in fashion and art drawing from French

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: croquis (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: croquis

croquis.notes: What a vivid studio metaphor: **un croquis** is a drawing 'bitten off' briskly from real life before the moment passes!

croustillant.etymology: Present participle of croustiller ('to crunch small crusts between the teeth'), formed in the 16th–17th century from croustille ('little crust'), diminutive of Old/Middle French crouste (modern croûte 'crust', from Latin crusta).

croûte.etymology: Inherited from Old French croste ('hard outer layer of bread or a wound'), from Classical Latin crusta ('hard surface, rind, shell, bark, crust').

history.meaning: hard outer rind, shell, or crust

crème.etymology: Inherited from Old French cresme ('rich fatty layer rising on milk'), from Late Latin chrisma ('consecrated anointing oil, chrism', borrowed from Ancient Greek khrisma 'unguent, anointing') blended in Gaul with Gaulish *crama ('cream of milk').

history.meaning: rich upper layer of milk, ointment

cuillère.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuillier ('spoon'), from Classical Latin cochlearium ('spoon with a pointed end for eating snails and eggs; measure of a spoonful'), derived from cochlea ('snail, spiral shell', from Greek kokhlias).

cuir.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuer / cuir ('skin, hide, tanned leather'), from Classical Latin corium ('thick hide of an animal, leather, rind').

cuire.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuire ('to cook, bake, burn, smart'), from Vulgar Latin *cocere, reduced from Classical Latin coquere ('to cook, bake, ripen, digest', from PIE *pekw-).

cuisine.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuisine ('kitchen, art of cooking, cooked food'), from Late Latin cocinae / coquina ('kitchen, art of cooking'), derived from coquus ('cook') and coquere ('to cook').

history.meaning: kitchen; style or art of cooking

cuisson.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuisson, from Vulgar Latin *coctionem (Classical Latin coctio, coctionis 'cooking, baking'), action noun of coquere ('to cook, bake').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cuisson (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cuisson

cuisson.notes: Whether asking how you'd like a steak cooked (**Quelle cuisson?**) or timing a brioche in the oven (**le temps de cuisson**), **la cuisson** is essential French kitchen vocabulary.

cuivre.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cuprum (shortened from aes Cyprium, 'metal of Cyprus', because the island of Cyprus had the Roman world's chief copper mines). Cuprum yielded Old French cuevre / cuivre—just as it gave English copper.

cognates.meaning: copper (early Germanic borrowing from Latin cuprum)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cuivre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cuivre

cultiver.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Medieval Latin cultivare ('to till the soil'), derived from Late Latin cultivus ('tilled, arable'), from Classical Latin cultus, past participle of colere ('to till, tend, inhabit, worship').

history.meaning: to cultivate soil, grow crops; to foster the mind

curieux.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (curios, 12th c., 'careful, eager to learn, inquisitive') from Classical Latin curiosus ('full of care, diligent, inquisitive, meddlesome'), derived from cura ('care, attention').

cèdre.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (cedre, 12th c.) from Classical Latin cedrus ('cedar tree, cedar oil'), from Ancient Greek kedros ('cedar, juniper').

céramique.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries from Ancient Greek keramikḗ (tékhnē) ('the potter's art'), from kéramos ('potter's clay, earthenware jar'), which also named the Kerameikós potters' quarter of ancient Athens.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: céramique (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: céramique

céramique.notes: Covers earthenware (**la faïence**), stoneware (**le grès**), and porcelain (**la porcelaine**).

côte.etymology: Inherited from Old French coste ('rib, side of the body, hillside, seacoast'), from Classical Latin costa ('rib, side, wall').

history.meaning: anatomical rib; steep slope, hill; seacoast

côté.etymology: Inherited from Old French costé ('flank, side'), from Vulgar Latin *costatum ('the ribbed part of the body, flank'), neuter noun formed on Classical Latin costa ('rib').

cœur.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuer ('heart, courage, inner mind'), from Classical Latin cor ('heart, soul, mind', from PIE *kerd- 'heart').

history.meaning: heart, seat of feeling and courage

d'abord.etymology: Adverbial phrase formed in the 16th century from de ('of, from') + abord ('approach, landing against a shore or ship', deverbal from aborder, built on bord 'side of a ship, shore') — originally 'at the very first contact or approach', hence 'at first, first of all'.

history.meaning: at first approach -> at first, first of all

d'accord.etymology: This expression combines the elided preposition de with accord, agreement. Accord itself is a noun formed from accorder. In the fixed expression, the combination expresses being in agreement.

dalle.etymology: Originally a Norman maritime and building word dale ('deck scupper trough; grooved flagstone channeled for rainwater; flat paving slab'), borrowed from Old Norse dœla ('small wooden gutter or trough aboard ship', related to dalr 'valley, hollow').

cognates.meaning: from related Old Norse dalr / Old English dæl ('valley')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: dalle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: dalle

dalle.notes: From Viking ship gutters in Normandy to cathedral and courtyard flagstones across France, **une dalle** traveled a remarkable journey.

dame.etymology: Inherited via Old French dame from Classical Latin domina ('mistress of a household, lady'), feminine counterpart of dominus ('master, lord', from domus 'house').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: dame (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: dame

dame.notes: **Madame** is simply the fused possessive phrase *ma dame* ('my lady').

danger.etymology: Inherited from Old French dangier ('arbitrary power of a feudal lord, dominion, mastery, resistance'), from Vulgar Latin *dominiarium, derived from dominium ('lordship, ownership', from dominus 'lord'); shifted from 'being at someone's mercy or power' (estre en son dangier) to 'peril, risk, danger'.

history.meaning: feudal mastery -> exposure to harm, peril, danger

dans.etymology: Dans comes from later Latin deintus, inside, composed from an intensive de- and intus, within. The Académie dates its French history to the twelfth century.

dansant.etymology: Present participle of danser ('to dance', from Old French dancier) used as an adjective meaning 'lively for dancing' or 'where dancing takes place' (as in une soirée dansante).

date.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Medieval Latin data ('indication of place and time on a document'), taken from the opening formula of Roman and medieval letters data (est epistola) Romae... ('[this letter was] given at Rome on...'), feminine past participle of dare ('to give, hand over to a courier').

history.meaning: calendar date of a document or event

de.etymology: De continues the Latin preposition de. Its older senses included separation and origin; later everyday Latin also expanded its use in partitive and possessive relationships. French inherited those connecting uses.

debout.etymology: Univerbation in Old/Middle French of the phrase de bout ('on end, upright'), from de ('of, on') + bout ('extremity, end', from Old French bouter 'to thrust, set').

history.meaning: standing on end -> upright, on one's feet, awake

dedans.etymology: Formed in Old French (dedenz, 11th c.) by reinforcing denz / dans ('inside, within', from Vulgar Latin *de intus 'from within') with a second initial preposition de.

degré.etymology: Inherited from Old French degré ('step of a staircase, rung, rank, gradation'), from Vulgar Latin *degradus, formed from de- + Classical Latin gradus ('step, pace, stair, rank').

history.meaning: stair step -> rank, level, unit of angle or temperature

dehors.etymology: Formed in Old French (defors / dehors, 11th c.) from de ('from, of') + hors (older fors, 'outside', from Classical Latin foris 'out of doors', related to forum and fores 'double doors').

demain.etymology: Demain developed from the later Latin expression de mane. That expression could refer to the morning and also to the morning of the following day; the latter reading became tomorrow.

demander.etymology: Demander comes from Latin demandare ('to entrust', and in Late Latin 'to request, ask for'). Unlike English 'demand', French demander is the polite everyday verb 'to ask'.

history.meaning: to entrust; Late Latin: to request

demander.notes: False friend: **demander** simply means 'to ask' (not 'demand', which is *exiger*).

demi.etymology: Inherited from Old French demi ('half'), from Vulgar Latin *dimedius, reshaped from Classical Latin dimidius ('halved, half'), compound of dis- ('apart') + medius ('middle').

demi-centimètre.etymology: Modern French compound noun formed from demi ('half') + centimètre ('centimeter').

demi-sel.etymology: Modern French culinary compound formed from demi ('half') + sel ('salt', from Latin sal), designating butter or fresh cheese lightly salted (typically 0.5% to 3% salt).

demi-tour.etymology: Compound noun formed from demi ('half') + tour ('turn, revolution') — literally 'a half-turn (180 degrees)', hence 'an about-face or turning back'.

demi-verre.etymology: Compound noun formed from demi ('half') + verre ('drinking glass', from Latin vitrum 'glass').

dentelle.etymology: Formed in the 16th century as a diminutive of dent ('tooth', from Classical Latin dentem); originally referred to the tiny tooth-like picots or scalloped points along the edge of openwork trimmings, before naming lacework as a whole.

depuis.etymology: Formed in Old French (depuis, 12th c.) from de ('from') + puis ('afterward, since', from Vulgar Latin *postius, comparative of Classical Latin post 'after, behind').

dernier.etymology: Dernier is a fifteenth-century contraction of derrenier, itself related to an older form ultimately derived from Latin deretro, behind. Its history connects being last with being at the back.

derrière.etymology: Inherited from Old French deriere ('behind, at the back'), from Late/Vulgar Latin de retro ('from behind, at the rear'), compound of de ('from, at') + retro ('backward, behind').

history.meaning: behind, in back of; rear end

descendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French descendre ('to come or go down, dismount'), from Classical Latin descendere ('to climb down, go down, sink'), compound of de- ('down from') + scandere ('to climb').

history.meaning: to go down, come down, get off; to carry down

desserrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (desserrer, 12th c.) from reversative prefix des- / dé- (Latin dis-) + serrer ('to press tight, lock, clench', from Late Latin serare 'to bolt, bar').

dessin.etymology: Deverbal noun from dessiner ('to draw, sketch, design'); originally spelled dessein in both senses ('mental plan/purpose' and 'graphic drawing') until the 17th–18th century split the spellings into dessein ('intention') and dessin ('drawing').

history.meaning: purpose, design -> graphic drawing, sketch, pattern

dessiner.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian disegnare ('to draw, outline, plan'), from Classical Latin designare ('to mark out, trace, point out'), from de- + signare ('to mark with a sign', from signum).

history.meaning: to mark out in lines, trace, draw

dessous.etymology: Formed in Old French (desoz, 11th c.) from de ('from, at') + souz / sous ('under, below', from Classical Latin subtus 'beneath, underneath').

dessus.etymology: Formed in Old French (desus, 11th c.) from de ('from, at') + sus ('up, above', from Vulgar Latin *susum < Classical Latin sursum 'upward, on high').

deux.etymology: Deux continues Latin duos, an object-case form of duo, two. The Académie records earlier French dos, dous and deus before the spelling deux.

deuxième.etymology: Deuxième was formed from deux ('two', from Latin duos) + the ordinal suffix -ième, providing a regular ordinal alongside older second.
deuxième.notes: Used interchangeably with *second(e)*, and preferred whenever a third (*troisième*) exists.

devant.etymology: Formed in Old French (devant, 11th c.) from de ('from, at') + avant ('in front, before', from Late Latin abante < ab + ante).

devenir.etymology: Inherited from Old French devenir ('to come to be, become'), from Classical Latin devenire ('to come down from, arrive at, reach a state'), from de- + venire ('to come').

deviner.etymology: Inherited from Old French deviner ('to practice divination, foretell, guess'), from Classical Latin divinare ('to foresee, prophesy, guess'), derived from divinus ('inspired by a god, prophetic', from divus / deus 'god').

history.meaning: prophetic -> to foretell by inspiration, guess
to foretell -> to guess, figure out

devoir.etymology: Devoir comes from Latin debere, to owe or be indebted. Its French use to express obligation is recorded from the ninth century. The noun meaning duty developed from the verb.

dieu.etymology: Inherited from Old French dieu ('God, a god'), from Classical Latin deus ('god, deity'), from PIE *deiwos ('celestial one, god', built on *dyew- 'bright sky, day').

dignité.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French dinité / dignité) from Classical Latin dignitatem (nominative dignitas, 'worthiness, merit, honorable rank'), derived from dignus ('worthy, deserving').

dimanche.etymology: Inherited from Old French diemenche ('Sunday'), from Ecclesiastical/Late Latin dies dominica (revised to *dia dominica, 'the Lord's day', translating Greek kyriake hemera), replacing pagan dies Solis ('day of the Sun').

dire.etymology: Dire continues Latin dicere, meaning to say or express something in words. The Académie dates the French verb to the tenth century. Declaring, naming and recounting are extensions of that central meaning.
dire.notes:
- Irregular: the *vous* form is *dites*, not *disez* (also *vous redites*, but *vous contredisez*).
- *Dire* is used with indirect speech: *dire que* + clause.

direction.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late/Classical Latin directionem (nominative directio, 'a making straight, aiming in a straight line'), action noun from dirigere ('to set straight, guide, direct').

history.meaning: setting in a straight line, guidance
line of movement, direction; management, steering

diriger.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin dirigere ('to set in a straight line, align, guide, steer'), compound of dis- / de- + regere ('to keep straight, rule, guide').

discours.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical/Late Latin discursus ('a running to and fro; in Late Latin, conversation, treatise, reasoning'), from discurrere ('to run about, treat of a subject').

history.meaning: running about -> orderly exposition in speech

discret.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Medieval/Ecclesiastical Latin discretus ('discerning, prudent, wise; separate, distinct'), originally the past participle of Classical Latin discernere ('to separate, distinguish, perceive clearly').

discrétion.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin discretionem (nominative discretio, 'separation, power of distinguishing, discernment, prudence'), derived from discernere, discretum.

history.meaning: good judgment, reserve, tact; free judgment (à discrétion)

disparaître.etymology: Formed in the 15th century (replacing Old French despareir) from prefix dis- ('away, reversal') + paraître ('to appear, come into view', from Vulgar Latin *parescere, inchoative of Classical Latin parere 'to appear').

history.meaning: to pass out of sight, vanish, disappear

dispute.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Middle French (originally 'formal scholastic debate', then 'heated argument, quarrel') from disputer ('to debate, argue').

disputer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin disputare ('to weigh or examine from all sides, discuss, debate'), compound of dis- ('apart, in different directions') + putare ('to reckon, consider, clear up').

history.meaning: to debate -> to contend for, quarrel, scold

distribuer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin distribuere ('to divide and deal out among several, apportion'), compound of dis- ('apart') + tribuere ('to assign, allot, grant').

divin.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin divinus ('of a god, godlike, prophetic, supremely admirable'), derived from divus ('god, deity', akin to deus).

diviser.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (replacing native Old French deviser in mathematical and physical senses) from Classical Latin dividere, divisum ('to force apart, separate into parts, distribute').

dix.etymology: Dix descends from Latin decem, ten. Eleventh-century French spellings included dis and diz.

dix-huit.etymology: Inherited from Old French dis et oit / dis-uit ('eighteen'), additive compound of dix ('ten', from Latin decem) + huit ('eight', from Latin octo), replacing Classical Latin subtractive duodeviginti ('two from twenty').

dix-neuf.etymology: Inherited from Old French dis et nuef / dis-nuef ('nineteen'), additive compound of dix ('ten', from Latin decem) + neuf ('nine', from Latin novem), replacing Classical Latin subtractive undeviginti ('one from twenty').

dizaine.etymology: Inherited from Old French disaine ('group of ten'), formed from dis / dix ('ten', from Latin decem) + collective numerical suffix -aine (from Latin -ena).

do.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century from Italian do, introduced by music theorists (traditionally linked to Giovanni Battista Doni or the syllable of Dominus 'Lord') as a more open, singable vowel to replace Guido d'Arezzo's original first solfège syllable ut.

history.meaning: first note of the diatonic scale (C)

doigt.etymology: Inherited from Old French doi ('finger'), from Classical Latin digitus ('finger, toe; inch-like measure'), respelled doigt in Middle French with silent etymological g and t after Latin digitus.

donc.etymology: Inherited from Old French donc / donques ('then, at that time; therefore'), from Vulgar Latin *dunc / *dumque, formed on Classical Latin dum ('while, then') blended with tunc ('then, at that time').

donner.etymology: Inherited from Old French doner ('to give'), from Classical Latin donare ('to present as a gift, bestow'), derived from donum ('gift'), which displaced irregular Classical Latin dare across Gaul.

history.meaning: to present with a gift -> to give

dormir.etymology: Dormir continues Latin dormire, to sleep. The Académie records the French verb from the twelfth century.

doré.etymology: Past participle of dorer ('to gild, coat with gold, brown to a golden hue'), inherited from Old French dorer, from Late Latin deaurare ('to gild over'), compound of de- + aurare (from aurum 'gold').

dos.etymology: Inherited from Old French dos ('back'), from Vulgar Latin *dossum, assimilation of Classical Latin dorsum ('back of a person or animal, ridge').

history.meaning: anatomical back, reverse or spine of an object

dossier.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from dos ('back') + suffix -ier; originally meant 'chair-back or headboard against which one leans one's back', and in the 18th century acquired the sense 'bundle of legal or administrative papers labeled on the back or spine (au dos)'.

history.meaning: chair-back -> bundle of papers labeled on the spine, file, case

double.etymology: Inherited from Old French doble ('twofold, double'), from Classical Latin duplus ('twofold, twice as much'), formed from duo ('two') + *-plos ('-fold').

doucement.etymology: Formed in Old French (doucement, 12th c.) from the feminine adjective douce ('sweet, soft, gentle', from Latin dulcis) + adverbial suffix -ment.

douche.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century from Italian doccia ('water pipe, gutter, jet of water poured over the body at thermal baths'), deverbal from docciare ('to pour in a stream'), from Vulgar Latin *ductia ('water conduit'), from Classical Latin ducere, ductum ('to lead, conduct').

douleur.etymology: Inherited from Old French dolor / douleur ('physical pain, grief, sorrow'), from Classical Latin dolorem (nominative dolor, 'ache, bodily pain, anguish'), derived from dolere ('to feel pain, grieve').

doux.etymology: Inherited from Old French douz (feminine douce, 'sweet to the taste, gentle, soft, mild'), from Vulgar Latin *dulcius, remodeled from Classical Latin dulcis ('sweet, pleasant, gentle').

douzaine.etymology: Formed in twelfth-century Old French (dozaine) from douze ('twelve', Latin duodecim) plus the collective numeral suffix -aine (from Latin -ena). English dozen was borrowed directly from Old French dozaine.

cognates.meaning: group of twelve (from Old French dozaine)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: douzaine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: douzaine

douze.etymology: Inherited from Old French doze ('twelve'), from Vulgar Latin *dodece, contracted from Classical Latin duodecim ('twelve', compound of duo 'two' + decem 'ten').

drap.etymology: Inherited from Old French drap ('woven woolen cloth, piece of fabric, bedsheet'), from Late Latin drappus ('piece of cloth', attested in the 6th-c. Capitularies and Oribasius), probably of Gaulish origin (*drappo-).

droit.etymology: Inherited from Old French dreit / droit ('straight, upright, right-hand; law, rightful claim'), from Vulgar Latin *derectus, syncopated from Classical Latin directus ('laid straight, direct, upright, just'), past participle of dirigere ('to set straight').

history.meaning: straight, right (not left); law, legal right

drôle.etymology: Appeared in the 15th–16th century as a noun meaning 'merry fellow, rascal, wag', probably borrowed from Middle Dutch drol ('little fat fellow, goblin, jester, bowling pin'); used as an adjective ('amusing, comical, odd') from the late 16th century.

du.etymology: Du is the contraction of de and the masculine singular article le. The ninth-century form del shows an earlier stage of the combination. Modern uses depend on whether the phrase expresses a relationship or an unspecified quantity.

duo.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian duo ('musical piece for two voices or instruments'), from Classical Latin duo ('two').

history.meaning: two -> musical piece for two performers
musical duet; pair of people working together

dur.etymology: Inherited from Old French dur ('hard, firm, harsh, difficult'), from Classical Latin durus ('hard to the touch, tough, stern, arduous', from PIE *deru- 'firm, solid like oak').

dès.etymology: Inherited from Old French des ('starting from, right from'), from Vulgar Latin *de ex, compound of Classical Latin de ('down from, from') + ex ('out of, directly from').

history.meaning: right out from, from the very moment or point of
from, right from, as early as

dé.etymology: In the sense of 'gaming die' and 'small cube' (un dé de carotte), inherited via Old French dé from Classical Latin datum ('that which is given or cast', neuter past participle of dare 'to give, throw'), used in Roman gaming slang for throwing dice.

history.meaning: something given or thrown (a cast of the dice)
die; small culinary cube (couper en dés)

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French dé / dés

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: dé (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: dé

dé.notes: Homonym note: **un dé à coudre** ('thimble') has a completely different origin—from Latin *digitale* ('finger cap', from *digitus* 'finger')!

débarrasser.etymology: Formed in the 16th century from reversative prefix dé- (Latin dis-) + embarrasser ('to obstruct, encumber with barriers') or directly on barras ('barrier, obstacle', from barre 'bar').

history.meaning: to clear away obstacles, free from encumbrance, clear the table

débloquer.etymology: Formed in the 16th–17th century from reversative prefix dé- + bloquer ('to blockade, jam, lock'); originally 'to raise a military siege', later 'to unjam a mechanism, unfreeze funds, unlock'.

history.meaning: to raise a blockade -> to unjam, unfreeze, unlock

début.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 16th century from débuter ('to play the first stroke toward the mark in bowls or billiards; to make one's first appearance'), itself formed from dé- + but ('target, goal, mark').

history.meaning: first throw toward the mark -> beginning, first appearance

décharger.etymology: Inherited from Old French deschargier ('to unload a burden, relieve of a duty or accusation'), formed from prefix des- / dé- + chargier / charger ('to load', from Late Latin carricare).

history.meaning: to unload cargo, relieve of a burden, discharge

déchirer.etymology: Inherited from Old French deschirer ('to tear apart, rend, scratch'), formed from intensive prefix des- (Latin dis-) + Frankish *skerian / Old High German skerran ('to scrape, scratch, tear', cognate with English shear).

history.meaning: to claw, rend, tear to pieces

décibel.etymology: Borrowed in the 1920s from English decibel, coined by telephone engineers at Bell Laboratories from metric prefix deci- ('one-tenth', from Latin decimus) + bel (unit named in honor of Alexander Graham Bell, 1847–1922).

history.meaning: one-tenth of a bel (logarithmic unit of sound intensity)

décision.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin decisionem (nominative decisio, 'a cutting off; a settlement, agreement'), derived from decidere ('to cut off; to settle a matter once and for all', from de- + caedere 'to cut').

décès.etymology: Décès was borrowed from Latin decessus, departure or death. The Académie records the French word from the eleventh century.

dégonfler.etymology: Formed in Middle/Modern French from reversative prefix dé- (Latin dis-) + gonfler ('to swell, inflate', from Vulgar Latin *conflare 'to blow up').

history.meaning: to deflate, let the air out of, reduce swelling

déjeuner.etymology: Déjeuner developed from a reconstructed Popular Latin verb *disjunare, shortened from *disjejunare, breaking a fast. Twelfth-century French used a reflexive form for taking the morning meal; in modern metropolitan French the usual meal is lunch.

déjà.etymology: Univerbation in Old/Middle French (des ja, 13th c.) of dès ('right from', < Vulgar Latin *de ex) + ja ('now, already', from Classical Latin jam 'now, already').

délicieux.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Late Latin deliciosus ('delightful, luxurious, dainty'), derived from Classical Latin deliciae ('delights, pleasures, luxuries', related to delicere 'to allure, entice').

démarrer.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century as a nautical verb ('to unmoor a ship, cast off') from reversative prefix dé- + amarrer ('to moor a vessel with cables', borrowed from Middle Dutch maren 'to tie, moor').

history.meaning: to untie mooring lines, cast off
to cast off -> to start moving, start up an engine

démonter.etymology: Formed in Old French (desmonter, 12th c., originally 'to unhorse a rider, throw from a mount') from prefix des- / dé- + monter ('to mount, go up, assemble'); extended in the 16th–17th century to taking apart an assembled mechanism.

history.meaning: to unhorse -> to take apart, disassemble; to disconcert

déménageur.etymology: Formed in the 19th century from déménager ('to move one's household goods to a new residence', from dé- + ménage 'household') + agent suffix -eur.

dénouer.etymology: Inherited from Old French desnoer ('to untie a knot, unravel'), formed from prefix des- / dé- (Latin dis-) + noer / nouer ('to tie in a knot', from Classical Latin nodare < nodus 'knot').

history.meaning: to untie a knot; to unravel a plot or crisis

départ.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (depart, 12th c., 'separation, division; act of leaving') from departir ('to divide, separate; to set out, leave', from Vulgar Latin *departire).

history.meaning: separation -> act of setting out, departure, start of a race

dépasser.etymology: Formed in Middle French from prefix dé- + passer ('to pass, step beyond', from Vulgar Latin *passare < passus 'step').

history.meaning: to go beyond, overtake, exceed, rise above

dépenser.etymology: Rebuilt in Middle French from dépense ('expenditure, pantry', from Late Latin dispensa, feminine past participle of dispendere 'to weigh out money, disburse'), replacing older dépendre ('to spend').

déplacer.etymology: Formed in Middle French (desplacer, 15th c.) from prefix des- / dé- + place ('place, spot') + verbal ending -er.

history.meaning: to move from its place, shift; (reflexive) to travel

déplier.etymology: Inherited from Old French despleier ('to unfold, spread open', doublet of déployer), from Late/Vulgar Latin displicare ('to unfold, scatter'), from dis- + plicare ('to fold').

dépoli.etymology: Past participle of dépolir ('to remove the polish or gloss from a surface'), formed in the 17th century from privative prefix dé- + polir ('to polish', from Latin polire).

history.meaning: deprived of gloss; frosted or ground (of glass)

dérangement.etymology: Formed in the 16th–17th century from déranger ('to throw out of order, disturb') + nominal suffix -ment.

déranger.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (desrengier, 13th c., 'to break military ranks, throw out of line') from prefix des- / dé- + rangier / ranger ('to set in a row or rank', from rang < Frankish *hring 'circle, ring of warriors').

history.meaning: to throw out of line -> to disarrange, disturb, bother

désolé.etymology: Désolé is the past participle of désoler, also used as an adjective. The Académie traces the verb to Latin desolare, to depopulate or devastate. The everyday apology uses a milder sense of distress or regret.

déterrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (desterrer, 12th c.) from prefix des- / dé- ('out of, away from') + terre ('earth, ground', from Latin terra) + -er.

history.meaning: to dig up out of the ground, unearth, unearth a secret

détester.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin detestari ('to curse while calling the gods to witness, execrate, abhor'), compound of de- ('away, down') + testari ('to call to witness, invoke', from testis 'witness').

history.meaning: to curse by calling the gods as witness, abhor
to execrate -> to hate intensely, detest

dîner.etymology: Inherited from Old French disner ('to take the first main meal of the day, break one's fast'), from Vulgar Latin *disjejunare ('to break one's fast', the tonic-accented doublet of déjeuner), formed from dis- + jejunare ('to fast', from jejunus 'fasting').

history.meaning: midday meal -> evening meal, dinner; to dine

eau.etymology: Eau descends intact through speech from Latin aqua ('water')! Intervocalic -qu- softened and dropped, leaving Old French ewe, eaue, modern eau — five Latin letters transformed into three vowels pronounced simply /o/.
eau.notes: **Eau chaude / froide** = hot / cold water; **eau gazeuse** = sparkling water.

elle.etymology: Elle continues Latin illa, the feminine of the demonstrative ille, that one. The Académie records ninth-century ele as a subject form and thirteenth-century elle as an object form. Modern elle can therefore be understood against a history with different grammatical uses and spellings.

emballer.etymology: Formed in the 14th century from prefix en- / em- ('in, into') + balle ('bale, tightly tied bundle of merchandise', from Frankish *balla 'ball, rounded bundle'); originally 'to pack goods into a bale', and figuratively in modern French 'to carry away with enthusiasm'.

history.meaning: to pack into a bale, wrap up; to thrill, get carried away

embaucher.etymology: Formed in the 16th century (originally in carpentry, 'to square a rough log into a beam', then 'to set a journeyman to work, hire') from em- ('in') + bauche / bauch ('squared timber beam; workshop', opposite of débaucher 'to entice away from the workshop').

history.meaning: to trim timber / bring into the workshop -> to hire, take on staff

embouteillage.etymology: Derived from embouteiller ('to pour wine into bottles', from en- + bouteille 'bottle' < Late Latin butticula 'small cask'); applied figuratively in Paris around the 1890s–1900s to vehicles wedged into a narrow street like liquid in a bottleneck.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: embouteillage (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

embouteillage.notes: Colloquial French carries the wine-bottle pun one step further by calling a traffic jam **un bouchon** ('a cork')!

emmener.etymology: Formed in Old French (enmener, 11th–12th c.) from adverbial pronoun en ('away from here', from Latin inde 'thence') + mener ('to lead, guide', from Late Latin minare).

history.meaning: to lead or take someone away with oneself

emprunter.etymology: Inherited from Old French emprunter ('to obtain as a loan, borrow'), from Vulgar Latin *improntare / *impromutuare, altered from Classical Latin in + promutuari ('to advance as a loan', from mutuum 'loan').

history.meaning: to borrow (money, an object, a word, or a route)

en.etymology: As a preposition, en descends from Latin in. It survives in many old fixed expressions, even where dans now serves other location senses. The pronoun en has a different Latin source, inde, from there.

encadrer.etymology: Formed in the 17th century from prefix en- ('in') + cadre ('square border, picture frame; staff of officers', borrowed from Italian quadro < Latin quadrum 'square') + -er.

history.meaning: to put in a frame, surround; to supervise or train a team

enchanté.etymology: Past participle of enchanter ('to cast a magic spell by singing, bewitch, delight'), inherited from Old French enchanter < Classical Latin incantare ('to chant a magic formula over'), from in- + cantare ('to sing'); used elliptically for je suis enchanté (de faire votre connaissance) as a polite greeting upon meeting someone.

history.meaning: to chant a spell over, bewitch

encore.etymology: Encore is traced to a reconstructed Popular Latin expression *hinc ha hora or *hinc ad horam, approximately from here until this hour. The French word is recorded from the eleventh century.

encre.etymology: Inherited from Old French enque / encre, from Late Latin encaustum ('purple ink used by Roman emperors'), borrowed from Ancient Greek énkauston ('burned in, heat-prepared pigment', from enkaíein 'to burn in') with proparoxytonic stress shift.

cognates.meaning: ink was borrowed from Old French enque

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: encre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: encre

encre.notes: English **ink** comes straight from the older Old French form **enque**, before French inserted an *-r-* to give **encre**.

endroit.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (en droit, 'right opposite, in the exact line of') of en ('in', < Latin in) + droit ('straight line, right side', < Latin directum); came to mean both 'a specific place or spot' and 'the right or finished side of a fabric'.

history.meaning: in the right line -> particular place, spot; right side of cloth

enfant.etymology: Inherited from Old French enfant ('young child; noble youth or page'), from Classical Latin infantem (nominative infans, 'speechless, newborn babe not yet able to speak'), compound of negative prefix in- ('not') + fans, present participle of fari ('to speak').

enfermer.etymology: Formed in Old French (enfermer, 11th c.) from prefix en- ('in, inside') + fermer ('to close, lock, make fast', from Classical Latin firmare 'to make firm, secure').

history.meaning: to shut or lock inside, enclose

enfin.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the Old French prepositional phrase en fin ('in the end, at last'), from en ('in', < Latin in) + fin ('end', < Latin finem).

history.meaning: in the end, at last, finally

enlever.etymology: Formed in Old French (enlever, 12th c.) from prefix en- (combining Latin in- and inde 'away') + lever ('to raise, lift', from Classical Latin levare); evolved from 'to lift up' to 'to carry off, abduct, remove, take off'.

history.meaning: to lift up -> to carry away, remove, take off

ennuyeux.etymology: Derived in Old French (enoios, 12th c., 'troublesome, vexing, wearisome') from ennui ('grief, vexation, boredom', from Old French enoi / enui, back-formed from enoiier < Late Latin inodiare 'to make hateful', from the phrase mihi in odio est 'it is hateful to me').

enrouler.etymology: Formed in Middle French from prefix en- ('in, around') + rouler ('to roll', from Old French roler < Vulgar Latin *rotulare, from rotula 'little wheel').

history.meaning: to roll up, wind or coil around

enseigne.etymology: Inherited from Old French enseigne ('mark, token, military banner, battle cry'), from Vulgar Latin *insignia (treated as a feminine singular noun from Classical Latin neuter plural insignia 'badges of office, standards, distinguishing marks', from signum 'mark, sign').

history.meaning: banner, standard -> shop sign, commercial brand

ensemble.etymology: Inherited from Old French ensemble ('together, at the same time'), from Vulgar Latin *insimul, reinforced from Classical Latin simul ('at the same time, together', cognate with English same and assemble); used as a noun ('harmonious whole, outfit, group') since the 16th century.

history.meaning: at the very same time, together
together (adv.); unified whole, matching outfit, musical group (noun)

ensuite.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the Old French phrase en suite ('in continuation, following right after'), from en ('in') + suite ('following, train, continuation', participial noun from suivre 'to follow').

history.meaning: in the train of -> next, afterward, then

entendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French entendre ('to direct one's attention or mind toward, understand, hear'), from Classical Latin intendere ('to stretch out, direct one's mind or ears toward, intend'), from in- + tendere ('to stretch'); displaced Old French oïr (< Latin audire) as the everyday verb for 'to hear'.

history.meaning: to stretch toward, direct attention to
to pay heed, understand -> to hear

enterrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (enterrer, 11th c.) from prefix en- ('in, into') + terre ('earth, ground', from Latin terra) + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: to put into the earth, bury, inter

entier.etymology: Inherited from Old French entier ('unbroken, whole, intact, upright'), from Classical Latin integrum (nominative integer, 'untouched, whole, complete', from in- 'not' + root of tangere 'to touch', learned doublet of intègre).

entourer.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from entour ('surroundings, circuit', from en + tour 'turn, circuit') + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: to form a circle around, surround, encircle

entre.etymology: Inherited from Old French entre ('between, among'), from Classical Latin inter ('between, among, during').

entrer.etymology: Inherited from Old French entrer ('to go inside, enter'), from Classical Latin intrare ('to go into, penetrate'), derived from intra ('inside, within').

history.meaning: to enter, come in, go in

entretien.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 15th century from entretenir ('to hold together, keep in good repair, support; to converse with', from entre- 'mutually' + tenir 'to hold').

history.meaning: upkeep, maintenance; formal conversation or interview

entrée.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle formed in Old French (entree, 12th c.) from entrer ('to enter').

history.meaning: act or place of entering, entrance, admission, starter dish

enveloppe.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old/Middle French from envelopper ('to wrap up, cover around').

history.meaning: outer wrapping or covering; folded paper letter envelope

envelopper.etymology: Inherited from Old French enveloper ('to wrap up, fold inside, entangle'), formed from prefix en- ('in') + root *vlopp- / *faluppa (found in Old French veloper / développe, from Late Latin faluppa 'chaff, bundle of straw or fibers, wrapping').

history.meaning: to wrap up in a bundle, enfold

envie.etymology: Inherited from Old French envie ('jealousy, begrudging; ardent desire, longing'), from Vulgar Latin *invidia for Classical Latin invidia ('envy, jealousy, ill will'), derived from invidere ('to look askance at, cast an evil eye upon', from in- + videre 'to look').

history.meaning: envy; strong wish, craving (avoir envie de)

envoyer.etymology: Envoyer continues later Latin inviare, to travel along or reach a place, which also developed the sense send. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

erreur.etymology: Erreur comes from Latin error, errorem ('wandering astray, mistake', from errare 'to wander, err'). Like most Latin abstract nouns in -or, it became feminine in French.
erreur.notes: **Par erreur** = by mistake; **mon erreur** uses *mon* before a vowel despite feminine gender.

escalier.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Old Provençal escalier (from Late Latin scalarium, built on scala 'ladder, flight of steps'). Earlier French used degré or montée; notice the prosthetic e- before sc- (compare scala -> échelle).
escalier.notes: **Monter / descendre l'escalier** = to go upstairs / downstairs.

espace.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French espace) from Classical Latin spatium ('room, expanse, distance, interval of time, racecourse').

history.meaning: open room, distance, interval of space or time
space, expanse, interval; printer's typographical space

espoir.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (espoir, 12th c.) from the stem of espérer ('to hope', Old French 1st-person singular espoir < Latin spero).

history.meaning: expectation of a desired good, hope

espèce.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin species ('outward appearance, form, sort, kind; in Late Latin, spices, coins, goods', from specere 'to look at, behold', doublet of épice).

history.meaning: kind, sort, biological species; (plural espèces) cash

espérer.etymology: Inherited from Old French esperer ('to hope, wait for'), from Classical Latin sperare ('to hope, look forward to', from spes 'hope'), later reshaped in spelling and stem vowels after the Latin model.

essai.etymology: Inherited from Old French essai ('test of metal or wine, trial, attempt'), from Late Latin exagium ('a weighing, balance, standard weight'), derived from exigere ('to drive out, weigh accurately, examine', from ex- + agere); immortalized in the literary sense by Montaigne's Essais (1580).

history.meaning: trial, test, attempt; literary essay (Montaigne, 1580); rugby try

essayer.etymology: Inherited from Old French essaier ('to test the quality of, put to the proof, attempt'), from Vulgar Latin *exagiare ('to weigh, test'), derived from Late Latin exagium ('a weighing').

history.meaning: to try, test, try on clothes

essuyer.etymology: Inherited from Old French essuier ('to dry off, wipe dry'), from Classical Latin exsucare ('to press or drain the juice/moisture out of'), compound of ex- ('out') + sucus ('juice, moisture').

history.meaning: to drain of moisture, dry off
to wipe dry, wipe; figuratively, to endure (a storm or refusal)

est.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (via Anglo-Norman est) from Old English east ('the east, direction of sunrise', from Proto-Germanic *austra-, cognate with Latin aurora 'dawn' from PIE *h2ews- 'to shine, dawn').

et.etymology: Et continues the Latin conjunction et, and. French had the ninth-century form e before the spelling was remodelled in the twelfth century; the written final t is not pronounced in the conjunction.

euh.etymology: Natural vocalic hesitation filler in spoken French, representing the mid central rounded vowel /ø/ or /ə/ uttered while pausing for thought.

euro.etymology: Coined and officially adopted by the European Council in Madrid (December 1995) as a clipping of Europe / européen for the single European currency introduced in 1999/2002.

history.meaning: unit of currency of the eurozone

exact.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin exactus ('weighed out, precise, accurate, finished'), past participle of exigere ('to drive out, measure, weigh accurately, demand').

exactement.etymology: Formed in the 16th century from the feminine adjective exacte ('accurate, exact') + adverbial suffix -ment.

excellent.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin excellentem (nominative excellens, 'rising above others, lofty, superior'), present participle of excellere ('to rise high, surpass, excel', from ex- + *cellere 'to rise, project', related to celsus 'high').

excuse.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Middle French (15th c.) from excuser ('to clear of blame, excuse', borrowed from Classical Latin excusare < ex- 'out of' + causa 'legal charge, accusation').

history.meaning: to free from a charge -> plea or apology offered to clear oneself

excuser.etymology: Excuser was borrowed from Latin excusare, to remove from blame, justify or excuse. The Académie records it from the twelfth century.

exemplaire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin exemplar ('model, pattern, transcript, copy') and Late Latin exemplarium ('copy of a book'), derived from exemplum ('sample, model, example').

history.meaning: model to imitate; transcribed copy of a text
serving as a model (adj.); single printed copy of a book or issue (noun)

expliquer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin explicare ('to unfold, unroll a scroll; to set forth clearly, expound'), compound of ex- ('out') + plicare ('to fold', learned doublet of éployer).

history.meaning: to unfold, unroll -> to make clear, expound

express.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-19th century as a railway term from English express (short for express train), itself borrowed earlier from Old/Middle French exprès ('sent for a special purpose, rapid', from Latin expressus).

history.form: expressus -> exprès -> English express -> French express
history.meaning: specially dispatched -> fast train, rapid delivery, espresso coffee

expéditeur.etymology: Formed in the 18th century from expédier ('to dispatch, send off goods or mail', from Classical Latin expedire 'to free the feet from a snare, make ready, dispatch') + agent suffix -teur.

history.meaning: person or firm that sends mail or freight, sender, shipper

expédition.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–15th century from Classical Latin expeditionem (nominative expeditio, 'a setting free, prompt dispatch of business, military campaign'), derived from expedire ('to extricate, make ready, dispatch', literally 'to free the foot', ex- + pes, pedis).

history.meaning: military or scientific expedition; shipping/dispatch of mail or goods

extérieur.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Classical Latin exteriorem (nominative exterior, 'outer, external'), comparative of exter / exterus ('on the outside, foreign'), from ex ('out of').

fa.etymology: Fourth syllable of the hexachord introduced by the medieval music theorist Guido d'Arezzo (c. 1025), taken from the initial syllable of the fourth half-line (Famuli tuorum) of the Latin hymn to St. John the Baptist Ut queant laxis.

history.meaning: fourth solfège note of the scale (F)

fabriquer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin fabricare / fabricari ('to fashion, build, forge, construct'), derived from fabrica ('workshop, artisan's trade', from faber 'smith, craftsman in hard materials', learned doublet of forger).

history.meaning: to fashion in a workshop, manufacture

face.etymology: Inherited from Old French face ('visage, countenance, front surface'), from Vulgar Latin *facia, reshaped from Classical Latin facies ('form, appearance, visage, face', related to facere 'to make, form').

history.meaning: front of the head, side of a coin or building, front (en face)

facile.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Classical Latin facilis ('easy to do, yielding, compliant'), derived from facere ('to do, make') — literally 'doable'.

facilement.etymology: Formed in the 15th century from the adjective facile ('easy') + adverbial suffix -ment.

facteur.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin factor ('maker, doer, creator', agent noun of facere 'to make, do'); first used in French for an artisan maker of musical instruments (facteur de pianos) and commercial agent, then in the 19th century for a mail carrier.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: facteur (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: facteur

facteur.notes: Remarkably, both Odette's world and the hotel's mail share this word: a piano builder is still called **un facteur de pianos**, while the person delivering postcards is **le facteur**.

faillir.etymology: Inherited from Old French faillir ('to miss one's aim, run short, fail, be on the verge of'), from Vulgar Latin *fallire, remodeled from Classical Latin fallere ('to deceive, slip, escape notice, fail').

history.meaning: to fail, default; (+ infinitive) to almost do something

faim.etymology: Inherited from Old French faim ('hunger'), from Classical Latin famem (nominative fames, 'hunger, famine').

faire.etymology: Faire continues Latin facere, to do or make. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. Both creating something and carrying out an action belong to its central meaning, which is why English may use either make or do depending on the construction.

fait.etymology: Fait comes regularly from Latin factum ('deed, thing done', neuter past participle of facere 'to do, make'), with Latin -ct- developing to French -it.
fait.notes: **En fait** = in fact, actually; **tout à fait** = quite, completely.
