falloir.etymology: Inherited from Old French faillir / faloir (originally the same verb as faillir < Vulgar Latin *fallire < Classical Latin fallere 'to be lacking, fail'); in impersonal constructions like il faut ('there is lacking -> there is need of -> one must'), it split off into a distinct defective verb of necessity.

history.meaning: to be lacking -> to be needed, be necessary

fameux.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin famosus ('much talked of, renowned; in Classical Latin also notorious'), derived from fama ('talk, rumor, reputation, fame', related to fari 'to speak').

familier.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th–13th century (Old French famelier) from Classical Latin familiaris ('belonging to a household, domestic, intimate, friendly'), derived from familia ('household').

famille.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin familia ('household establishment, including servants and relatives under one roof'), derived from famulus ('household servant').

history.meaning: household retinue, family under one roof

fantastique.etymology: Fantastique was borrowed through later Latin fantasticus from Greek phantastikos, capable of forming images or imagining illusions. The French adjective is recorded from the fourteenth century.

faute.etymology: Inherited from Old French faute ('lack, scarcity, failure, misstep'), from Vulgar Latin *fallita ('a failing, shortcoming'), feminine participial noun from *fallire (Classical Latin fallere 'to fail, err').

history.meaning: lack (faute de); error, mistake, moral fault, sports foul

fendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French fendre ('to cleave, split lengthwise, crack'), from Classical Latin findere ('to cleave, split, divide').

fenêtre.etymology: Fenêtre comes from Latin fenestra ('window, opening for light'). The circumflex over ê marks the Old French s that disappeared before t (compare English 'defenestrate').
fenêtre.notes: **Regarder par la fenêtre** = to look out through the window.

fer.etymology: Inherited from Old French fer ('iron, iron tool or weapon, horseshoe'), from Classical Latin ferrum ('iron; any iron implement or sword').

fer-blanc.etymology: Compound attested since the 16th century from fer ('iron' < Classical Latin ferrum) + blanc ('white, gleaming bright' < Frankish *blank), naming thin sheet iron dipped in molten tin so it gleams silvery-white and resists rust.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fer-blanc (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fer-blanc

fer-blanc.notes: Classic French biscuit tins, tea caddies, and childhood keepsake boxes are traditionally made of **fer-blanc**.

ferme.etymology: As an adjective ('firm, steadfast, solid'), inherited from Old French ferm < Classical Latin firmus ('strong, stable, steadfast'); as a noun ('farmhouse, leased agricultural estate'), derived from Medieval Latin firma ('fixed rent payment, lease contract', from firmare 'to confirm, fix').

history.meaning: steadfast, solid; land held on a fixed lease

fermer.etymology: Inherited from Old French fermer ('to make fast, fortify, lock, shut'), from Classical Latin firmare ('to make firm, strengthen, secure'); in French it gradually replaced clore (< claudere) as the everyday verb for 'to close, shut'.

history.meaning: to fasten, lock -> to close, shut

fermeture.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from fermer ('to close, fasten, lock') + nominal suffix -ure (modeled on ouverture).

history.meaning: act or mechanism of closing; closure, fastener, zipper (fermeture éclair)

feu.etymology: Inherited from Old French fue / feu ('fire'), from Classical Latin focus ('hearth, domestic fireplace'), which in Popular Latin displaced ignis as the everyday word for 'fire' across all Romance languages.

history.meaning: fire, flame, traffic light, stove burner

feuille.etymology: Inherited from Old French fueille ('leaf of a plant, sheet'), from Vulgar Latin *folia, originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin folium ('leaf, sheet'), reanalyzed as a feminine singular collective noun.

history.meaning: tree leaf; sheet of paper or metal

feutre.etymology: Inherited via Old French feltre from West Germanic / Frankish *filtir ('pressed wool, felt'). Medieval Latin Latinized this same Germanic word as filtrum—giving French filtre and English filter, because liquids were strained through pads of wool felt!

cognates.meaning: native Germanic cognate / Medieval Latin derivative

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: feutre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: feutre

feutre.notes: From *feutre* also comes the adjective **feutré** ('muffled, hushed', like footsteps on felt or a felt piano hammer).

fiable.etymology: Inherited from Old French fiable ('trustworthy, reliable', revived in the 20th century under the influence of English reliable), formed from se fier ('to trust, confide in', from Vulgar Latin *fidare < fidus 'trustworthy') + suffix -able.

ficelle.etymology: Inherited from Old French ficele ('thin cord, string'), from Vulgar Latin *fiscella (Classical Latin fiscella 'small basket woven of slender rushes', crossed in Gallo-Romance with filum 'thread').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ficelle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ficelle

ficelle.notes: In French bakeries, **une ficelle** is also a slender, extra-crisp cousin of the **baguette**, half as wide and twice as crunchy.

fiche.etymology: Deverbal noun from ficher ('to drive in, fix, pin fast'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *figicare, frequentative of Classical Latin figere ('to fasten, pierce'); shifted from a peg/slip pinned onto a board to a catalog or recipe card.

history.meaning: index card, catalog slip, recipe card

cognates.meaning: microfiche borrowed directly from French fiche

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fiche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fiche

fiche.notes: Notice the family resemblance between **une fiche** (a card slipped into a file) and **une affiche** (a notice posted on a wall)!

fidèle.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century (replacing native Old French feil / féal) from Classical Latin fidelis ('trustworthy, faithful, loyal, true'), derived from fides ('trust, faith, loyalty').

fier.etymology: As an adjective ('proud, haughty, noble'), inherited from Old French fier < Classical Latin ferus ('wild, untamed, fierce, bold'); as a reflexive verb (se fier 'to trust'), inherited from Old French fier < Vulgar Latin *fidare (from Classical Latin fidus 'faithful').

fil.etymology: Inherited from Old French fil ('spun thread, yarn, wire, cutting edge'), from Classical Latin filum ('thread, string, cord, contour line').

history.meaning: thread, wire, blade edge, continuous thread of a story or call

film.etymology: Film is a nineteenth-century borrowing from English film, originally a membrane or thin covering. The material sense provided the name for the photographic medium and later for the work recorded on it.

fin.etymology: Combines two converged words: (1) noun fin ('end, boundary, purpose'), inherited from Old French fin < Classical Latin finis ('boundary, limit, end'); and (2) adjective fin ('pure, refined, slender, subtle'), derived in Old French from Latin finis ('the highest degree or perfection of something').

history.meaning: end, conclusion (noun); refined, thin, keen, delicate (adj.)

final.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Late Latin finalis ('relating to the end, concluding, decisive'), derived from Classical Latin finis ('end, limit').

finalement.etymology: Formed in the 13th–14th century from the feminine adjective finale ('final') + adverbial suffix -ment.

history.meaning: in the end, finally, after all

fini.etymology: Past participle of finir ('to finish, complete, end'), used as an adjective ('finished, completed, bounded, finite') and noun ('the finite, quality of polished workmanship').

finir.etymology: Inherited from Old French fenir / finir ('to bring to an end, conclude, die'), from Classical Latin finire ('to bound, limit, bring to an end'), derived from finis ('boundary, end').

history.meaning: to set bounds to, bring to an end

fissure.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin fissura ('cleft, chink, narrow crack'), derived from findere, fissum ('to cleave, split').

fixer.etymology: Derived in the 14th–15th century (originally in alchemy, 'to render a volatile substance solid or non-volatile') from the adjective fixe ('fastened, stationary', from Classical Latin fixus, past participle of figere 'to fasten, drive in').

history.meaning: fastened -> to make fast, fasten, set a date/price, stare at

flamme.etymology: Inherited/re-Latinized from Old French flame / flambe ('blazing tongue of fire'), from Classical Latin flamma ('blazing fire, flame, passion', from *flagma, akin to flagrare 'to blaze').

fleur.etymology: Inherited from Old French flor / fleur ('blossom, flower; finest part or prime'), from Classical Latin florem (nominative flos, 'flower, blossom, crown', from PIE *bhleh3- 'to blossom').

history.meaning: flower, blossom, surface level (à fleur de)

fleuriste.etymology: Formed in the 17th century from fleur ('flower') + specialist suffix -iste; originally denoted an amateur cultivator or painter of rare flowers before meaning a flower seller.

history.meaning: cultivator or seller of flowers, florist

fleuve.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French flueve) from Classical Latin fluvius ('river, running stream'), derived from fluere ('to flow'); in modern French geography, specifically distinguishes a major river flowing into the sea from a tributary (rivière).

history.meaning: major river emptying into the sea

flèche.etymology: From twelfth-century Old French fleche ('arrow'), generally traced via Old Low Franconian *fliugika ('flying shaft', related to Germanic *fleugan 'to fly'). Extended to church spires and later to drawn directional pointers.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: flèche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: flèche

foi.etymology: Inherited from Old French fei / foi ('trust, pledged word, religious faith'), from Classical Latin fidem (nominative fides, 'trust, confidence, honesty, sworn word', from PIE *bheidh- 'to trust, persuade').

fois.etymology: Fois continues Latin vices, turns or alternations, the plural of an otherwise unused form reconstructed as *vix. Tenth-century French had feiz. The modern word counts occurrences.

foncé.etymology: Past participle of foncer; in the color sense ('deep, dark-toned', as in bleu foncé), attested since the 17th century, evolving from 'deepened, sunk to the bottom (fond)' or 'saturated with a heavy base coat of pigment'.

fond.etymology: Inherited from Old French fonz / fond ('bottom, lowest part, depth'), from Classical Latin fundus ('bottom of a vessel, sea, or valley; piece of landed property', from PIE *bhudhn- 'bottom', cognate with English bottom).

history.meaning: bottom, back part, background, core substance

fontaine.etymology: Inherited from Old French fontaine ('natural spring of water; monumental water fountain'), from Late Latin fontana (originally feminine of adjective fontanus 'of a spring', supplying aqua 'spring water'), from Classical Latin fons, fontis ('spring, fountainhead').

forcer.etymology: Inherited from Old French forcier ('to overpower by strength, compel, break open'), derived from force ('physical strength, violence', from Late Latin fortia, neuter plural of fortis 'strong').

history.meaning: strength -> to compel by force, strain, break open

forcément.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from forcé ('compelled, inevitable', past participle of forcer) + adverbial suffix -ment.

history.meaning: of necessity, inevitably, bound to be

former.etymology: Inherited/adapted in the 12th century from Classical Latin formare ('to shape, fashion, mold, instruct'), derived from forma ('shape, mold, form').

formidable.etymology: Formidable was borrowed from Latin formidabilis, inspiring fear, related to formido, terror. The French word originally concerned something frightening before developing its familiar favourable sense.

fort.etymology: Inherited from Old French fort ('physically strong, sturdy, valiant, intense'), from Classical Latin fortis ('strong, powerful, brave, steadfast').

history.meaning: strong, loud, skilled (adj.); fortress (noun); very, hard (adv.)

fortune.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin fortuna ('chance, luck, fate, good or bad fortune, wealth', personified as the goddess Fortuna), derived from fors, fortis ('chance, luck', from PIE *bher- 'to carry, bring').

forêt.etymology: Inherited from Old French forest, from Carolingian Medieval Latin (silva) forestis ('unenclosed royal woodland lying outside park walls'), derived from Classical Latin foris ('outdoors, outside').

history.meaning: open royal woodland outside fenced enclosures

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: forêt (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: forêt

forêt.notes: The circumflex in **forêt** preserves the memory of the *s* still pronounced in **forestier** ('forestry') and English *forest*.

fouetter.etymology: Derived in Middle French from fouet ('whip, whisk'), itself the diminutive of Old French fou ('beech tree', from Latin fagus), because a fouet was originally a supple thin beech switch!

morphemes.meaning: beech tree (Old French fou < Latin fagus)

history.meaning: to whip; to whisk cream or eggs

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fouetter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fouetter

fouetter.notes: In a French kitchen, the wire balloon whisk itself is simply called **un fouet**.

fouiller.etymology: Inherited from Old French foillier ('to root or dig in the earth like a boar, rummage'), from Vulgar Latin *fodiculare ('to dig repeatedly, poke, root around'), frequentative of Classical Latin fodere ('to dig').

history.meaning: to dig about, root in the ground
to excavate, search thoroughly, rummage through

four.etymology: Four descends from Latin furnus ('oven, furnace') via Old French forn, four; final n dropped after r (though derivatives like fourneau and boulanger's fournil kept the n).
four.notes: **Sorti du four** = fresh out of the oven.

fourneau.etymology: Inherited from Old French fornel ('small oven, hearth, stove'), diminutive of four ('oven', from Classical Latin furnus).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fourneau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fourneau

fourneau.notes: To be busy cooking for guests is idiomatically **être aux fourneaux**.

frais.etymology: As an adjective ('cool, fresh, newly made', fem. fraîche), inherited from Old French freis / fresche, borrowed from Frankish *frisk ('fresh, untainted, cool', cognate with English fresh); as a plural noun (des frais 'expenses, costs'), from Medieval Latin fredum ('peace-fine paid to a magistrate', from Frankish *frithu 'peace').

fraise.etymology: Inherited from Old French frese / fraise ('wild strawberry'), from Vulgar Latin *fraga (originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin fragum 'strawberry', reinterpreted as a feminine singular noun, with intervocalic -g- > -y- / -z-).

history.meaning: strawberry; ruffled collar (16th c.); rotary milling cutter

franc.etymology: Inherited from Old French franc ('free by birth, noble, sincere, candid'), from Late Latin Francus ('a Frank; under Frankish rule in Gaul, a free man exempt from tributary servitude', from Proto-Germanic *Frankon); the coin name franc comes from the 1360 gold coin inscribed Francorum Rex ('King of the Franks').

history.meaning: a Frank -> free man, noble, candid
free, candid, outspoken (adj.); French currency unit (noun)

franchement.etymology: Formed in Old French (franchement, 12th c., originally 'freely, nobly', then 'openly, candidly') from the feminine adjective franche ('free, frank, sincere') + adverbial suffix -ment.

franchir.etymology: Derived in Old French (franchir, 12th c.) from franc ('free, unhindered'); originally meant 'to set free, exempt', then evolved in the 16th century to 'to clear an obstacle freely at a single bound, cross over a threshold or boundary'.

history.meaning: to set free -> to leap clear over an obstacle, cross a boundary

frapper.etymology: Inherited from Old French fraper ('to strike, hit, beat'), formed on an expressive or Germanic root *frapp- / *hrapp- imitating a sharp blow or lash.

history.meaning: to strike, hit, knock at a door; to chill with ice; to impress deeply

fredonner.etymology: Derived in sixteenth-century French from fredon ('musical trill, vocal ornament, refrain'), an expressive onomatopoeic formation imitating rapid hummed notes.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fredonner (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fredonner

friable.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (by Bernard Palissy) from Classical Latin friabilis ('easily crumbled or broken into small pieces'), derived from friare ('to rub, crumble, break into small pieces').

history.meaning: crumbly, friable (of rock, soil, or pastry)

frigo.etymology: Colloquial 20th-century clipping (with popular -o suffix) of frigorifique ('refrigerating apparatus, cold storage', coined in the 19th century from Latin frigorificus < frigus, frigoris 'cold' + -ficare 'to make').

froid.etymology: Froid descends from Popular Latin *frigidus / *frigdu ('cold', Classical Latin frigidus). Loss of the unstressed vowel and palatalisation of -gd- produced Old French freit, froit, modern froid.
froid.notes: **Avoir froid** = to feel cold (of a person); **refroidir** = to cool down.

fromage.etymology: Fromage comes from Late Latin *(caseus) formaticus — 'cheese shaped in a mould' (from forma 'mould, form'). Through metathesis of r, Old French formage became modern fromage, while Italian formaggio kept the original order.
fromage.notes: Same Latin phrase gave Italian *formaggio* and Catalan *formatge*.

froncer.etymology: Inherited from Old French froncier ('to wrinkle, pleat, pucker'), from Frankish *hrunkjan ('to wrinkle, crease', related to Old High German runza 'wrinkle', with initial Germanic hr- rendered as fr- in Gallo-Romance).

history.meaning: to pleat fabric; to knit the brow (froncer les sourcils)

front.etymology: Inherited from Old French front ('forehead, brow; front line of an army'), from Classical Latin frontem (nominative frons, 'forehead, brow, forepart').

frotter.etymology: Inherited from Old French froter ('to rub, chafe, scrub'), probably from Vulgar Latin *frictare, frequentative built on Classical Latin fricare, frictum ('to rub').

fruit.etymology: Inherited from Old French fruit ('produce of the earth or trees, fruit, profit'), from Classical Latin fructus ('enjoyment, proceeds, produce, fruit of a tree or crops', from frui 'to enjoy, have the use of').

history.meaning: edible plant fruit; outcome or reward of labor

frère.etymology: Frère descends from Latin frater, fratrem ('brother'), with regular lenition of intervocalic -tr- to -r- through Old French frere.
frère.notes: **Grand frère / petit frère** = older / younger brother.

fuir.etymology: Inherited from Old French fuïr ('to flee, run away from danger'), from Vulgar Latin *fugire, remodeled from Classical Latin fugere ('to flee, take flight', from PIE *bhewg-).

history.meaning: to flee, shun; (of a pipe or roof) to leak

fuite.etymology: Inherited from Old French fuite ('act of fleeing, flight'), from Vulgar Latin *fugita, feminine participial noun formed on *fugire (Classical Latin fugere 'to flee').

history.meaning: flight, escape; leak of water, gas, or secret information

fusain.etymology: Inherited via Old French fusain ('spindle tree') from Vulgar Latin *fusago, *fusaginem, derived from Classical Latin fusus ('spinning spindle'), because its dense fine wood was prized first for carving spindles and later for charring into artists' charcoal sticks.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fusain (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fusain

fusain.notes: Even when modern charcoal sticks are made from willow twigs, French artists still call every charcoal drawing **un dessin au fusain**.

fusible.etymology: Originally a fourteenth-century learned adjective from Medieval Latin fusibilis ('capable of melting', from fundere, fusum 'to melt, pour'). In late nineteenth-century electricity, un coupe-circuit fusible was shortened to un fusible: the calibrated wire designed to melt first and protect the circuit.

history.meaning: safety fuse in an electrical circuit

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fusible (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fusible

fâché.etymology: Past participle of fâcher ('to anger, displease, vex'), inherited from Old/Middle French faschier ('to weary, disgust, annoy'), from Vulgar Latin *fasticare, contracted from Classical Latin fastidiare ('to feel loathing or distaste', from fastidium 'aversion, weariness').

history.meaning: angry, cross, sorry, on bad terms

félicitations.etymology: Plural of félicitation ('act of wishing someone joy or congratulating them'), derived in the 17th century from féliciter ('to congratulate').

history.meaning: expressions of joy for another's success, congratulations

féliciter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical/Late Latin felicitare ('to make happy'), derived from felix, felicis ('happy, fortunate'); shifted in 17th-century French from 'to make happy' to 'to congratulate someone on their good fortune'.

gagner.etymology: Inherited from Old French gaaignier ('to till the soil, forage, capture booty, earn by labor'), borrowed from Frankish *waidanjan ('to pasture, forage, hunt for food', from *waida 'pasture, hunting').

history.meaning: to harvest, earn -> to win, gain, reach

gamme.etymology: Inherited from Old French game / gamme ('musical scale'), from Medieval Latin gamma, the Greek letter G (Γ) placed by Guido d'Arezzo at the bottom of the medieval musical scale to denote the lowest bass note (gamma ut, which also gave English gamut).

history.meaning: lowest note of Guido's hexachord -> entire musical scale
musical scale; full range or product line

gant.etymology: Inherited from Old French guant / gant, borrowed from Frankish *want ('glove, hand-wrapping', related to Germanic *windan 'to wind, wrap around').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French gantelet ('little/armored glove')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: gant (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: gant

gant.notes: Initial Frankish *w-* regularly became *gu-* -> *g-* in French (just as *wardon* gave **garder** and *werra* gave **guerre**).

garder.etymology: Inherited from Old French garder ('to watch over, protect, keep'), borrowed from Frankish *wardon ('to stand guard, watch over, protect', from Proto-Germanic *wardona, cognate with English ward and guard).

history.meaning: to guard, look after, keep, retain

gare.etymology: Gare originally meant a sheltered river dock where boats pulled aside (from garer 'to moor, shelter', of Frankish origin *waron 'to watch out, protect'). In the railway age, river-dock terminology transferred directly to train stations!
gare.notes: For bus or tram stops, French says **un arrêt**; for metro, **une station**; for trains, **la gare**.

garer.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century (originally in river navigation, 'to berth a boat in a sheltered cove or dock out of the main current') from Old Occitan garar ('to watch out, shelter, protect'), itself from Frankish/Gothic *waron ('to heed, protect', cognate with gare 'river basin -> railway station').

history.meaning: to shelter, put in a safe berth
to dock a boat, shunt a train -> to park a car

garçon.etymology: Inherited from Old French garçon (originally the oblique case of gars, meaning 'serving-boy, camp-follower, valet, young lad'), from Frankish *wrakjo ('retainer, mercenary, exile, young warrior', cognate with English wretch).

gauche.etymology: Gauche emerged in Middle French, probably from gauchir ('to veer aside, bend', from Frankish *wenkjan 'to waveringly turn aside', cognate with English 'wink' and 'flinch'), replacing older senestre ('left').

gazeux.etymology: Formed in the late 18th century (Lavoisier, 1787) from gaz ('gas', coined by the Flemish chemist J. B. van Helmont in the 17th c. after Greek khaos 'chaos, air') + adjectival suffix -eux.

history.meaning: gaseous; carbonated, sparkling (of water or drinks)

genre.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French gendre / genre) from Classical Latin genus, generis ('birth, descent, race, stock, kind, sort, grammatical gender', from PIE *gene- 'to give birth, beget').

history.meaning: kind, sort, artistic genre, grammatical gender, manner

gens.etymology: Inherited from Old French gent (plural genz / gens, 'race, nation, people, folk'), from Classical Latin gentem (nominative gens, 'clan, Roman patrician family, tribe, people', from PIE *gene- 'to beget').

gilet.etymology: Appeared in the 17th–18th century for a sleeveless waistcoat; traditionally traced either to Gille (the stock comic buffoon of French fairground theater who wore a sleeveless jerkin) or via Spanish jileco / Algerian Arabic jalika from Turkish yelek ('sleeveless vest').

glace.etymology: Inherited from Old French glace ('ice'), from Vulgar Latin *glacia, feminine singular reshaped from Classical Latin glacies ('ice'); extended in the 16th–17th century to polished plate-glass mirrors and to frozen desserts (ice cream).

history.meaning: ice; plate-glass mirror or car window; ice cream

glacé.etymology: Past participle of glacer ('to freeze, turn to ice, chill, coat with a glossy sugar icing'), derived in Old French from glace ('ice').

history.meaning: frozen, icy cold; glazed, glossy, iced

glaçage.etymology: Formed in the 18th–19th century from glacer ('to glaze, coat pastry with shiny sugar icing') + nominal suffix -age.

history.meaning: glossy finishing glaze; sugar icing or frosting on a cake

glisser.etymology: Inherited from Old French glier / glicier ('to slip, slide, glide'), borrowed from Frankish *glidan ('to glide, slip smoothly', cognate with English glide) crossed with Old French glacier ('to slip on ice', from glace).

history.meaning: to slide, slip, glide, slip something in discreetly

gond.etymology: Inherited via Old French gont from Late Latin gumphus / gomphus ('iron hinge pin, peg, joint'), borrowed from Ancient Greek gómphos ('wooden peg, iron bolt, molar tooth').

history.meaning: vertical iron pintle supporting a door or shutter

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: gond (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: gond

gond.notes: Because a shutter lifted off its *gonds* swings out of control, **sortir de ses gonds** means 'to lose one's temper'—literally 'to come off one's hinges'!

gonflé.etymology: Past participle of gonfler ('to blow up, swell, inflate'), inherited via Old French / Occitan gonflar from Classical Latin conflare ('to blow together, blow up a fire or bladder'), from com- + flare ('to blow').

gorgée.etymology: Formed in Old French (gorgiee, 12th c.) from gorge ('throat, gullet', from Late Latin gurga < Classical Latin gurges 'whirlpool, abyss, throat') + suffix -ée denoting the amount swallowed at one time.

history.meaning: a mouthful or swallow of liquid, sip, gulp

goutte.etymology: Inherited from Old French gote ('drop of liquid; trace amount, nothing at all in ne... goutte; gout'), from Classical Latin gutta ('falling drop of liquid').

goûter.etymology: Inherited from Old French goster ('to taste, sample food or drink'), from Classical Latin gustare ('to taste, take a little of, enjoy'), derived from gustus ('taste, sipping'); as a noun (le goûter), denotes the light afternoon snack.

goûteur.etymology: Formed in Middle/Modern French from goûter ('to taste, test food or wine') + agent suffix -eur.

gramme.etymology: Borrowed in 1793–1795 by the founders of the French metric system from Late Latin gramma / Ancient Greek gramma ('written character; small weight equal to one twenty-fourth of an ounce, scruple'), from graphein ('to write').

history.meaning: base metric unit of mass (weight of one cubic centimeter of water)

grand.etymology: Grand comes from Latin grandis ('full-grown, tall, great'), which completely displaced Classical Latin magnus in spoken Gallo-Romance.
grand.notes: Before a vowel or mute h, liaison sounds final d as /t/ (*un grand hôtel* /ɛ̃ ɡʁɑ̃t‿otɛl/).

grand-mère.etymology: Compound kinship noun formed in Old/Middle French from grand ('great, elder', retaining its archaic invariable feminine form grand without -e from Latin grandis) + mère ('mother', from Latin matrem).

grand-père.etymology: Compound kinship noun formed in Middle French (replacing older aïeul) from grand ('great, elder', from Latin grandis) + père ('father', from Latin patrem).

grandir.etymology: Inherited from Old French grandir ('to grow tall, increase, make great'), from Vulgar Latin *grandire (for Classical Latin grandescere), derived from grandis ('large, tall, full-grown').

history.meaning: to grow up, grow taller, increase

gratter.etymology: Inherited from Old French grater ('to scratch, scrape, claw'), borrowed from Frankish *kratton ('to scratch, scrape', from Proto-Germanic *krattōną, cognate with German kratzen and English scratch).

gratuit.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Classical Latin gratuitus ('done without pay or profit, spontaneous, free of charge'), derived from gratia ('favor, kindness, thanks') and gratis ('for nothing').

history.meaning: done out of favor without payment, free
free of charge; unprovoked or unfounded (of an act or claim)

gratuitement.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from the feminine adjective gratuite ('free of charge, unprovoked') + adverbial suffix -ment.

history.meaning: free of charge, for nothing; without justification

grave.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century (replacing native Old French grief in most senses) from Classical Latin gravis ('heavy, weighty, serious, deep in pitch, pregnant', from PIE *gwerh2- 'heavy').

history.meaning: serious, solemn, severe; low-pitched (in music); grave accent (`)

graver.etymology: Inherited from Old French graver ('to make a part in the hair; to incise, carve into wood, stone, or metal'), borrowed from Frankish *graban ('to dig,hollow out, carve', from Proto-Germanic *grabana, cognate with English grave and engrave).

history.meaning: to engrave, carve, etch; to burn a disc or memory

grenier.etymology: Grenier descends from Latin granarium ('granary, grain loft above a house', from granum 'grain'). Because grain was stored dry under the rafters, le grenier became the everyday word for an attic.
grenier.notes: Compare English 'granary' and 'garner' (borrowed from Old French).

grille.etymology: Inherited from Old French greïlle / grille ('iron gridiron for broiling; grating of iron bars'), from Late Latin craticula ('small hurdle, fine gridiron'), diminutive of Classical Latin cratis ('wickerwork hurdle, lattice, harrow').

history.meaning: iron grating, wrought-iron gate; crossword or schedule grid

grimper.etymology: Appeared in the 15th century ('to climb up by clutching with hands and feet'), altered with nasalization from Old French griper ('to seize, clutch with claws'), borrowed from Frankish *gripan ('to grip, clutch', cognate with English grip and gripe).

history.meaning: to clutch with hands or claws -> to climb, clamber up

grincement.etymology: Formed in the 16th century from grincer ('to gnash the teeth, creak, grate', from Old French grincier < Frankish *grinitjan 'to snarl, bare or gnash the teeth') + nominal suffix -ment.

history.meaning: gnashing of teeth; harsh grating or squeaking sound

gris.etymology: Inherited from Old French gris ('gray; gray squirrel fur'), borrowed from Frankish *gris ('gray', from Proto-Germanic *grisaz, cognate with Old Saxon gris and German greis 'hoary, gray-haired').

gros.etymology: Inherited from Old French gros ('thick, bulky, coarse, large'), from Late Latin grossus ('thick, coarse, big', attested from the 4th c.), which replaced Classical Latin crassus for physical bulk.

grâce.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (grace, 12th c.) from Classical Latin gratia ('favor, esteem, charm, goodwill, thanks; in Christian Latin, divine grace'), derived from gratus ('pleasing, welcome, thankful').

grès.etymology: From twelfth-century Old French gres ('gritstone, sandstone, cobblestone'), borrowed from Old Low Franconian *greot ('coarse sand, gravel'—cognate with Old English greot, modern English grit). Later applied to dense, high-fired stoneware pottery whose vitrified body is as hard as sandstone.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: grès (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: grès

guide.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Old Occitan guida or Italian guida ('person who shows the way'), deverbal noun from guidar / guidare ('to guide, direct'), itself from Gothic/Frankish *witan ('to watch over, show the way, direct').

history.meaning: to show the way -> leader, guide
person who leads the way; guidebook, mechanical guide-rail

guêpe.etymology: Guêpe developed from reconstructed Gallo-Romance *wespa, a blend of Latin vespa and Frankish *waspa, both meaning wasp. The Académie records twelfth-century wespe.

gâteau.etymology: Gâteau descends from Old French gastel ('fine round loaf, cake'), borrowed from Frankish *wastil ('food, pastry'). As s before t fell silent and vocalised -el became -eau, gastel became gâteau (compare English 'wastel-bread').

génial.etymology: Génial was borrowed from Latin genialis, associated with birth or festivity and related to genius. Its sixteenth-century French senses included fruitful or pleasant, before its modern uses for brilliance or enthusiastic approval.

génie.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin genius ('tutelary deity or guardian spirit of a person or place, innate nature or inclination', from gignere 'to beget'); in the 17th–18th century expanded to mean 'extraordinary creative endowment' and (by convergence with ingénieur/engin) 'military or civil engineering'.

history.meaning: tutelary spirit -> supreme creative genius; engineering corps

généreux.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin generosus ('of noble birth, high-minded, magnanimous'), derived from genus, generis ('birth, noble stock'); evolved from 'nobly born, gallant' (as in Corneille) to 'liberal in giving, open-handed'.

ha.etymology: Natural primary interjection attested since Old French (ha / a), expressing sudden surprise, relief, laughter, or realization.

history.meaning: exclamation of surprise, laughter, or sudden emotion

habiter.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin habitare ('to dwell, reside continually in a place'), frequentative of habere ('to have, hold').

history.meaning: to have continually -> to dwell, inhabit

habituer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late Latin habituare ('to bring into a condition or habit'), derived from Classical Latin habitus ('condition, bearing, dress, acquired habit', from habere 'to have, hold').

history.meaning: to give a settled disposition or habit to

heure.etymology: Heure continues Latin hora, hour, a borrowing from Greek hôra, a period of time. The Académie records the eleventh-century French form ure. The word’s earlier history concerns a period or division of time, rather than only the modern clock display.

histoire.etymology: Histoire was borrowed from Latin historia (from Ancient Greek historía 'inquiry, narrative, account'). Mute h triggers elision and liaison: *l'histoire*, *mon histoire*.

horloge.etymology: Horloge descends via Old French orloge from Latin horologium and Ancient Greek hōrológion ('instrument that tells the hour', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell').
horloge.notes: Mute h: **l'horloge** (feminine), unlike a wristwatch (**une montre**).

horloger.etymology: Agent noun formed in Middle French from horloge ('clock') + -er, with horloge coming via Latin horologium from Ancient Greek hōrológion ('hour-teller', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell, read out').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: horloger (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: horloger

horloger.notes: Unlike *hêtre*, the *h* in **l'horloger** and **l'horloge** is Latin-Greek and completely mute.

huile.etymology: Inherited via Old French oile / uile from Classical Latin oleum ('olive oil'), borrowed from Ancient Greek élaion (from elaía 'olive tree'). Medieval French scribes added a silent initial h- purely so manuscript readers would not misread uile as vile ('vile, cheap'), since u and v were written with the same letter!

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French oile before graphic h- was added

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: huile (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: huile

huile.notes: The exact same scribal trick explains silent *h-* in **huit** (*uit* vs *vit*), **huître** (*uistre* 'oyster'), and **huis** (*uis* 'door', as in *à huis clos*)!

hêtre.etymology: Borrowed via Old and Middle French hestre from Frankish *haistr ('young beech sapling', compare Middle Dutch heester). It gradually replaced Old French fou (< Latin fagus) because fou had become homophonous with fou ('mad, crazy')!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: hêtre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: hêtre

hêtre.notes: Because it comes from Germanic rather than Latin, **le hêtre** keeps an *h* aspiré (never *l'hêtre*!).

hôtel.etymology: Hôtel descends from Medieval Latin hospitale ('guest quarters, hostel'), neuter substantive of hospitalis ('relating to a guest or host', from hospes). Old French ostel meant a lodging or town residence; the circumflex in hôtel marks the lost s that English kept in hostel and hospital.
hôtel.notes: Compare **hôtel de ville** ('town hall') and **hôpital** (learned doublet from the same Latin root).

ici.etymology: Ici combines an initial element from Old French iluec, there, with ci. The Académie dates the word to the eleventh century.

idée.etymology: Idée continues Latin idea, borrowed from Greek idea, visible form, kind or category, related to the Greek verb for seeing. The Académie records the twelfth-century French form idees.

il.etymology: Il developed from later Latin pronoun forms illi and illum, continuing Classical Latin ille and illud, that person or that thing. The Académie dates the French pronoun to the ninth century. A demonstrative used to point something out became a third-person subject pronoun.

improviser.etymology: Improviser is a seventeenth-century borrowing from Italian improvvisare, with the same sense of producing something without prior preparation.

impôt.etymology: Inherited from Old French impost, from Medieval/Classical Latin impositum ('assessment or charge laid upon', substantivized neuter past participle of imponere 'to place upon').

history.meaning: to lay upon -> charge laid upon

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Middle French impost / imposer

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: impôt (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: impôt

impôt.notes: As always in French spelling, the circumflex on **impôt** marks the historical *-s-* of Old French **impost**.

indice.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin indicium ('disclosing sign, token, proof'), related to index ('forefinger, pointer') and indicare ('to point out, make known').

history.meaning: to point out -> revealing sign, clue

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: indice (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: indice

indice.notes: False-friend alert: English *index* (at the back of a book) is **un index** in French too, whereas **un indice** primarily means a 'clue' or 'revealing sign'!

interrupteur.etymology: Adapted in nineteenth-century physics and electrical engineering from Latin interruptor ('one who breaks off', from interrumpere 'to break between, interrupt'): a switch opens or closes a gap in the electrical current.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: interrupteur (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: interrupteur

itinéraire.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin itinerarium ('road map, travel account'), derived from Classical Latin iter, itineris ('walk, road, journey', related to ire 'to go').

cognates.meaning: from the same Late Latin stem

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: itinéraire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: itinéraire

itinéraire.notes: On French road signs, **Itinéraire bis** marks a scenic or secondary detour route avoiding holiday traffic!

ivoire.etymology: Inherited through Old French ivurie / ivoire from Latin eboreus ('made of ivory', from ebur 'ivory'—itself borrowed via Egyptian ābu 'elephant, ivory').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ivoire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ivoire

jamais.etymology: Jamais combines Old French ja ('already, ever', from Latin iam) + mais ('more', from Latin magis): literally 'ever more'. Paired with ne, it came to mean 'never'.
jamais.notes: Without *ne* in questions (*Si jamais...*), it can still mean 'ever'.

jardin.etymology: Jardin comes from Gallo-Roman *hortus gardinus ('enclosed garden'), built on Frankish *gardo ('enclosure, yard', cognate with English 'yard' and 'garden'). Old French jardin passed straight into English 'garden' via Norman.

je.etymology: Je descends from Late Latin eo, itself continuing Classical Latin ego, I. The Académie dates the French pronoun to the eleventh century. Its earlier Latin forms help explain a history that is not obvious from the very short modern word.

jeudi.etymology: Jeudi developed from Latin Jovis dies, day of Jupiter. The Académie records the twelfth-century form juesdi.

journée.etymology: Journée is derived from jour, day. The twelfth-century form journee already belongs to this French word family.

jusque.etymology: Jusque descends from Latin inde usque ('from there all the way to'), blending de + usque ('all the way, continuously') into Old French jusque, jusques.
jusque.notes: Usually elides before *à* or *au*: **jusqu'à demain**, **jusqu'au deuxième étage**.

juste.etymology: Juste was borrowed from Latin justus, just or right. The adjective is recorded from the twelfth century; adverbial uses such as just or only developed alongside it.

lait.etymology: Lait comes from Popular Latin *lacte (Classical Latin lac, lactis, 'milk'). The Latin -ct- cluster regularly palatalised to -it in French (compare noctem -> nuit, factum -> fait).
lait.notes: Gives **le laitier** ('milkman, dairy') and **café au lait**.

laiton.etymology: From Old French laton / laiton ('brass, copper-zinc alloy'), attested across medieval Western Romance and Mediterranean trade (compare Arabic lāṭūn 'copper/brass'), reshaped in French under the influence of lait ('milk') because of the pale sheen of freshly polished brass.

cognates.meaning: medieval sheet brass (from Old French laton)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: laiton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: laiton

lampe.etymology: Lampe comes via Late Latin lampada from Ancient Greek lampás, lampádos ('torch, oil lamp', from lámpein 'to shine').
lampe.notes: **Lampe de chevet** = bedside lamp; **lampe de poche** = pocket flashlight.

lanterne.etymology: Lanterne comes from Latin lanterna ('lantern, torch'), itself an early borrowing (via Etruscan) from Ancient Greek lamptḗr ('torch, lamp', from lámpein 'to shine').
lanterne.notes: Shares its ultimate Greek root 'to shine' with **la lampe**.

larme.etymology: Inherited via Old French lairme / larme from Classical Latin lacrima (archaic Old Latin dacrima), descending from the same Indo-European root as English tear.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: larme (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: larme

larme.notes: Colloquially in French cafés and kitchens, **une larme de lait / de miel** also means 'just a tiny drop' in a cup.

le.etymology: The article le and feminine la continue object-case forms of Latin demonstratives ille and illa. The direct-object pronouns le and la share that historical source, although articles and pronouns do different jobs today.

lentille.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin lenticula ('lentil'), diminutive of Classical Latin lens, lentis ('lentil'). In the seventeenth century, physicists named curved optical glass 'lentilles' (and English 'lenses' directly from Latin lens) because a biconvex glass disc is shaped just like a lentil seed.

cognates.meaning: from Old French lentille / directly from Latin lens

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lentille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lentille

lentille.notes: In French, eyeglass lenses in frames are usually called **les verres de lunettes**, while contact lenses and camera lenses are **des lentilles**.

lettre.etymology: Lettre comes from Latin littera ('written character', and in the plural litterae 'epistle, written message'), evolving through Old French letre into both French lettre and English 'letter'.

libraire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin librarius ('copyist of manuscripts, bookseller'), derived from liber ('inner bark of a tree used for writing; book').

cognates.meaning: shifted in English to 'public/lending collection', whereas French librairie kept 'bookshop'

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: libraire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: libraire

libraire.notes: Classic false friend: **un / une libraire** sells books in **une librairie** ('bookshop'), while a librarian in **une bibliothèque** is **un / une bibliothécaire**.

lierre.etymology: Formed in Middle French by agglutinating the elided definite article l' onto Old French ierre ('ivy'): l'ierre ('the ivy') was reanalyzed by speakers as a single noun le lierre! Old French ierre itself came regularly from Classical Latin hedera ('ivy').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lierre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lierre

lierre.notes: The same article fusion created French **le lendemain** ('the next day', from *l'endemain*) and **la luette** ('uvula', from *l'uette*).

lin.etymology: Inherited via Old French lin from Classical Latin linum ('flax plant, linen thread, linen cloth'), cognate with Ancient Greek línon.

cognates.meaning: lingerie comes from French linge (< lineus 'made of linen')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lin (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lin

lin.notes: Normandy and northern France remain among the world's premier growers of flax (**le lin**), woven into tablecloths, bookbinding thread, and summer clothes.

lit.etymology: Lit descends regularly from Latin lectus ('couch, bed'): -ct- developed to -it and short e merged into i, producing Old French and modern French lit (with silent final t).
lit.notes: Gives **la literie** ('bedding'); **faire le lit** = to make the bed.

loquet.etymology: Diminutive formed in twelfth-century Old French from loc ('lock, bolt'), an early borrowing from Old English loc or Frankish/Old Norse lok ('fastener, bar, lock'). English latch and lock belong to the very same Germanic family.

cognates.meaning: lock; small hinged case (locket borrowed back from French loquet)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: loquet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: loquet

lui.etymology: Lui continues Latin illi, a dative form of the demonstrative ille or illa. The Académie records ninth-century li. Modern lui can be an indirect-object form or a stressed pronoun.

lunettes.etymology: Lunette is the diminutive of lune ('moon', from Latin luna): a 'little moon' first meant a small round mirror or round glass lens in the Middle Ages, and in the plural **lunettes** came to mean a pair of eyeglasses.
lunettes.notes: Always plural for spectacles: **mes lunettes**, **une paire de lunettes**.

lutherie.etymology: Formed from luthier ('maker and repairer of stringed instruments'), derived from luth ('lute') < Old French leüt, borrowed via Old Occitan/Spanish from Arabic al-ʿūd ('the wood; the oud/lute').

cognates.meaning: all trace back to Arabic al-ʿūd

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lutherie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lutherie

lutherie.notes: Even after violins eclipsed lutes in the 17th century, French kept **luthier** and **lutherie** for all bowed and plucked wooden instruments.

là.etymology: Là comes from Latin illac or illa, by that way or there. It is recorded in French from the eleventh century.

madame.etymology: Madame combines ma, my, and dame, lady. The Académie records this form of address from the twelfth century.

mais.etymology: Mais developed from Latin magis, more or rather. The French word is recorded from the tenth century; its history helps explain the move from preference or contrast to but.

manche.etymology: Feminine la manche ('sleeve') is inherited from Classical Latin manica ('long tunic sleeve reaching over the hand, handcuff'), derived from manus ('hand').

history.meaning: shirt or coat sleeve; narrow sea channel (la Manche)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: manche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: manche

manche.notes: Masculine **le manche** ('broom or pan handle') comes from a closely related Latin derivative *manicus* ('part held in the hand').

manteau.etymology: Manteau comes from Latin mantellum ('cloak, cloth covering') via Old French mantel; vocalisation of final -el before plural -s produced manteau (compare English 'mantle' and 'mantelpiece').

mardi.etymology: Mardi continues Latin Martis dies, day of Mars. The twelfth-century French form marsdi preserves the older name more visibly.

marge.etymology: Adapted in Old and Middle French from Classical Latin margo, marginem ('edge, border, riverbank').

history.meaning: blank border of a page; leeway

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old/Middle French or directly from Latin marginem

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marge (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marge

marge.notes: French school notebooks famously feature a red vertical line marking **la marge** on the left side of every squared page.

marmite.etymology: From Middle French marmite ('deep lidded cooking pot'), substantivized feminine of Old French adjective marmite ('demure, secretive, hiding one's face'), humorously applied to a covered pot that conceals what simmers inside.

cognates.meaning: named after the French earthenware cooking pot pictured on its label

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marmite (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marmite

marmite.notes: In French home cooking, **faire bouillir la marmite** ('keep the soup pot boiling') idiomatically means 'to keep the household fed and running'.

marteau.etymology: Inherited from Old French martel, from Late Latin martellus ('hammer'), diminutive of Imperial Latin martulus (an alteration of Classical Latin marculus 'small smith's hammer').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marteau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marteau

marteau.notes: Around 1709 Bartolomeo Cristofori invented the *gravicembalo col piano e forte* by replacing harpsichord plucks with tiny leather-and-felt **marteaux**.

menthe.etymology: Inherited via Old French mente from Classical Latin mentha ('mint'), borrowed from Ancient Greek mínthē (in myth, the nymph Minthe transformed into the fragrant herb).

cognates.meaning: early West Germanic borrowing from Latin mentha

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: menthe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: menthe

menthe.notes: Hot green **thé à la menthe** steeped with fresh spearmint leaves is a beloved café staple across France.

menton.etymology: Inherited via Old French menton from Vulgar Latin *mentonem, enlarged from Classical Latin mentum ('chin', from an Indo-European root *men- 'to jut out', also seen in promontoire and éminent).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: menton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: menton

menton.notes: Watch out for the look-alike verb **mentir** ('to tell a lie', from Latin *mentiri* 'to fabricate in the mind' < *mens*) — completely unrelated to **le menton**!

merci.etymology: Merci comes from Latin merces, which meant pay or a price and later favour or grace. The Académie records ninth-century mercit with the sense of grace or mercy. Modern merci is the everyday expression of thanks; the older sense survives in sans merci.

history.meaning: pay, price; later favour or grace

merci.notes:
- Answer to *merci* is usually *de rien* or *je vous en prie*.
- *Non, merci* declines an offer; *Oui, merci* accepts it.

meuble.etymology: Shortened from biens meubles ('movable goods'), inherited from Spoken Latin *movibilis (Classical Latin mobilis, 'movable', from movere 'to move'). In medieval law property was either immeuble ('immovable': land and buildings) or meuble ('movable': chests, tables, beds).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: meuble (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: meuble

midi.etymology: Midi combines the older French elements mi, middle, and di, day. They descend from Latin medius and dies. The combination originally identifies the middle of the day.

miel.etymology: Miel comes directly from Latin mel ('honey'), with regular diphthongisation of stressed short e into ie (as in caelum -> ciel).

miette.etymology: Double diminutive formed in Old French from mie ('soft inner crumb of bread, tiny bit') + -ette, inherited from Classical Latin mica ('crumb, grain of salt, tiny morsel').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: miette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: miette

miette.notes: Modern French still distinguishes **la croûte** ('crust'), **la mie** ('soft inside of the loaf'), and **les miettes** ('loose crumbs').

mijoter.etymology: Attested from Middle/Classical French in regional northern usage (originally 'to coddle, store fruit gently in straw or crumbs to ripen', then 'to cook very slowly over low heat'), expressive derivative built on Old French mie / Picard mijot.

history.meaning: to simmer slowly over gentle heat

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mijoter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mijoter

mijoter.notes: Figuratively, **Qu'est-ce que vous mijotez?** means 'What scheme or surprise are you cooking up?'.

mille.etymology: The number mille was borrowed from Latin mille, thousand. Its French history is recorded from the eleventh century; the number does not take an ordinary plural s.

minuit.etymology: Compound inherited from Old French mienuit ('the middle of the night'), combining feminine mie (< Latin media 'middle') and nuit (< Latin noctem 'night'), exactly parallel to midi (< medius dies 'midday').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: minuit (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: minuit

minuit.notes: Originally feminine because *nuit* is feminine, **minuit** shifted to masculine on the model of **midi**.

minute.etymology: The time word minute comes from medieval Latin minuta, a noun use of the feminine of minutus, small. The Académie records it from the thirteenth century. The separate document-draft sense has its own specialised history.

miroir.etymology: Miroir comes from Old French mireor, built on mirer ('to look at, gaze at', from Latin mirari 'to wonder at, admire'). English 'mirror' was borrowed directly from Old French.
miroir.notes: **Regarder dans le miroir** = to look in the mirror.

moi.etymology: Moi continues Latin me, me. The Académie records ninth-century French mi. It is the stressed object form rather than the subject form je.

moineau.etymology: Diminutive in -eau (Old French moignel) of moine ('monk' < Late Latin monachus), affectionately naming the house sparrow after the brown-and-grey hood of its plumage, which reminded medieval observers of a friar's cowl.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: moineau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: moineau

moineau.notes: Older French called a sparrow **un passereau** (from Latin *passer*), which survives in **les passereaux** ('songbirds'), while cheeky little **moineau** ('little monk') won everyday speech!

mon.etymology: Mon and its feminine counterpart ma descend from Latin meus, mea and meum. The Académie records tenth-century mo. Modern forms agree with the possessed noun rather than naming the owner’s gender.

monde.etymology: Monde, world, descends from Latin mundus with the same meaning. It is recorded from the twelfth century. The rare adjective monde, clean, is a different dictionary entry.

monter.etymology: Monter comes from later Latin montare, to go up, derived from mons or montis, mountain. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century; riding and mounting are related extensions.

montre.etymology: Montre is a noun built from montrer ('to show, display', from Latin monstrare). It first named a shop display case and the visible dial that 'showed' the hours, before naming a pocket watch or wristwatch.

mortier.etymology: Inherited via Old French mortier from Classical Latin mortarium ('stone or wooden trough in which lime and sand — or kitchen herbs — are pounded together; the mortar mixed in it').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French mortier and Latin mortarium

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mortier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mortier

mortier.notes: Just as in English, **un mortier** means both the mason's lime-and-sand mix between flagstones and the kitchen mortar used with a pestle (**un pilon**).

motus.etymology: Playful 17th-century mock-Latin interjection built on French mot ('word' < Late Latin muttum 'muttered sound') + humorous Latinate ending -us, popularized in classical comedy for '(not a) word! hush!'.

history.meaning: not a word! mum's the word!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: motus (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: motus

motus.notes: Because of its mock-Latin disguise, the final *-s* of **motus** **/mɔtys/** is always pronounced aloud, especially in the beloved idiom **Motus et bouche cousue!** ('Mum's the word and lips sealed!').

muet.etymology: Old French diminutive built on mu ('mute, silent', from Latin mutus) + -et. As one-syllable mu risked homophony in speech, the fuller form muet replaced it completely by Middle French.

cognates.meaning: silent (from Latin mutus / Old French muet)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: muet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: muet

mystère.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek mystḗrion ('secret rite, hidden truth'), derived from mýstēs ('initiate') and mýein ('to close the eyes or lips').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mystère (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mystère

mystère.notes: Note the medieval homograph: Old French *mestier* ('craft, guild', modern **métier**, from Latin *ministerium*) was sometimes spelled *mystère* when craft guilds staged medieval 'mystery plays'!

mélodie.etymology: Learned borrowing via Late Latin melodia from Ancient Greek melōidía ('singing, choral song, tune'), compounded from mélos ('limb; musical phrase') and ōidḗ ('song', source of ode).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mélodie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mélodie

nappe.etymology: Nappe comes from Latin mappa ('napkin, signal cloth'), with dissimilation of initial m- to n- before -pp- in Popular Latin *nappa. English 'napkin' and 'apron' (originally 'a napron') both come from this French word!
nappe.notes: False friend: **la nappe** is a tablecloth; a napkin is **une serviette**.

ne.etymology: The negative ne continues Latin non. Its French history is recorded from the tenth century. The chemical abbreviation Ne belongs to an unrelated Greek-derived name.

non.etymology: Non continues Latin non. The Académie analyses the older Latin expression as *ne oinum, not a single one; the asterisk marks a reconstructed earlier form.

notre.etymology: Notre comes from Latin noster, our. Ninth-century French had nostro. Modern plural nos belongs to this same possessive series.

nous.etymology: Nous descends from Latin nos, meaning we or us. The Académie dates the French pronoun to the ninth century. Modern nous still has both subject and object uses, so its history fits a wider range than the single English gloss we.

nouveau.etymology: Nouveau descends from Latin novellus, young or recent, itself related to novus, new. Twelfth-century French had novel; the alternative nouvel preserves that older shape.

nouvelle.etymology: The noun nouvelle, news, comes from Latin novella, a noun use of the neuter plural of novellus, new or recent. Its plural use for news should be distinguished from the adjective nouvelle and from the later literary sense short story.

noyer.etymology: Inherited from Spoken Latin *nucarius ('walnut tree'), derived from Classical Latin nux, nucis ('nut, walnut'—which itself gave French noix). Like chêne or merisier, the tree name also names its timber.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: noyer (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: noyer

noyer.notes: An accidental homograph of the verb **noyer** ('to drown', from Latin *necare*), which has a completely separate origin.

nuit.etymology: Nuit continues Latin nox, with the stem noct-. The Académie records tenth-century noit before the modern spelling.

oh.etymology: Oh is an expressive interjection recorded in French from the sixteenth century. The Académie considers borrowing from the same Latin exclamation probable, rather than presenting that route as certain.

oignon.etymology: Inherited from Old French oignon, from Classical Latin unionem (accusative of unio, 'oneness, single large pearl; country Latin word for a single-bulb onion', contrasted with multi-clove garlic).

cognates.meaning: onion was borrowed from Old French oignon; union is its learned Latin doublet!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: oignon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: oignon

oignon.notes: Old French wrote *oign-* to represent palatal /ɲ/ after *o*; the 1990 spelling reform also permits **ognon** to match modern pronunciation /ɔɲɔ̃/.

ombre.etymology: Inherited directly from Classical Latin umbra ('shadow, shade'), with regular Romance lowering of short Latin u to /o/ nasalised before m + consonant.

cognates.meaning: little shade (via Italian ombrello from Latin umbra)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ombre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ombre

on.etymology: On descends from Latin homo, meaning a human being. The Académie records om in the ninth century and hom or hum in the eleventh. A noun referring to a person became a subject pronoun; its older noun-like construction also explains l’on.
on.notes: The possessive can depend on the meaning: general on can go with son/sa/ses; when on means nous, notre/nos is common.

orage.etymology: Inherited from Old French orage (originally 'strong wind, gust of air'), from Vulgar Latin *auraticum, built on Classical Latin aura ('breeze, breath of air', borrowed from Greek aúra).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: orage (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: orage

orage.notes: Unrelated to *or* ('gold')—its initial *or-* reflects Latin *au-* (*aura* -> *or-*), just as *aurum* gave *or*.

oreille.etymology: Inherited from Classical/Colloquial Latin auricula ('earlobe, little ear'), diminutive of Classical Latin auris ('ear'). Across all Romance languages, spoken Latin preferred the expressive diminutive auricula over short auris.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: oreille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: oreille

oreille.notes: Adding *-er* to *oreille* produced **un oreiller**—literally 'the thing for your ear', i.e. a pillow!

orteil.etymology: Inherited from Old French arteil ('toe'), from Classical Latin articulus ('little joint, knuckle, digit'), whose initial vowel shifted from a- to o- in Gallo-Romance through the influence of Gaulish ordiga ('big toe').

cognates.meaning: learned doublet of orteil from Latin articulus

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: orteil (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: orteil

orteil.notes: Few pairs look more surprising than **un orteil** ('a toe') and **un article** ('a newspaper article'), yet both trace back to Latin *articulus*!

oui.etymology: Oui developed from Old French oïl, an affirmative response. The Académie dates the modern form to the fourteenth century.

ouvert.etymology: Ouvert is the past participle and adjective of ouvrir ('to open'), descending from Vulgar Latin *opertus (for Classical Latin apertus 'open, uncovered').
ouvert.notes: Feminine **ouverte** sounds the final t (/uvɛʁt/). English 'overt' was borrowed from Old French.

ouvrir.etymology: Ouvrir descends from Vulgar Latin *operire (a blend of Classical Latin aperire 'to open' with cooperire 'to cover', which gave couvrir). Intervocalic -p- voiced and softened to -v-.
ouvrir.notes: Conjugates like a -er verb in the singular present (*j'ouvre, tu ouvres, il ouvre*) despite its -ir infinitive; past participle **ouvert**.

où.etymology: Où descends from Latin ubi, where. The Académie records the French question word from the tenth century.

pain.etymology: Pain descends from Latin panis ('bread, loaf'). From Old French onward it has stood at the centre of daily meals and expressions such as gagner son pain ('to earn one's living') and copain (literally 'one who shares bread').

panier.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin panarium ('breadbasket'), derived from panis ('bread', French pain) + -arium. Long after baskets came to carry everything at market, the word still preserves 'bread' at its core.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: panier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: panier

papier.etymology: Papier comes via Latin papyrus from Ancient Greek pápyros ('Nile papyrus sedge, writing sheet'), shifting in the late Middle Ages to rag-and-pulp paper.

parler.etymology: Parler continues Christian Latin parabolare, to speak, related to parabola, speech. That word was borrowed from Greek parabolê, comparison or parable. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

partition.etymology: From Latin partitio ('division into parts', from partiri 'to divide'). In seventeenth-century music (matching Italian partitura), une partition meant dividing an ensemble piece onto aligned staves on one page so every voice or hand could be read together—hence 'musical score / sheet music'.

history.meaning: musical score arranged in aligned staves

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: partition (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: partition

pas.etymology: The negative pas began as the noun for a step, from Latin passus. It first strengthened negatives with movement verbs by referring to even a tiny distance, then became a general spoken negative marker.

passer.etymology: Passer comes from a reconstructed later Latin *passare, derived from passus, step. The Académie records the French verb from the eleventh century.

patrimoine.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin patrimonium ('inheritance passed down from a father', from pater, patris 'father'). Expanded in modern French from family estate to shared cultural and architectural heritage (le patrimoine historique).

perdre.etymology: Perdre descends from Latin perdere, originally to give wastefully and later to destroy or ruin. The Académie records the French verb from the ninth century.

persil.etymology: Inherited via Old French perresil / persil from Late Latin petrosilinum, borrowed from Ancient Greek petrosélinon ('rock celery', compound of pétra 'rock' + sélinon 'celery, parsley').

petit.etymology: Petit is traced to a Gallo-Romance form *pit- expressing smallness. Medieval Latin pititus provides evidence for that family; the reconstructed base is marked with an asterisk.

peu.etymology: Peu continues Latin paucum, few or little. Early French spellings included pou, poi and po before peu became established.

peut-être.etymology: Peut-être joins peut, the he/she present form of pouvoir, and être, to be. Twelfth-century expressions included put cel estre and puet estre; the hyphenated form is recorded in the seventeenth century.

pharmacien.etymology: Formed in Classical French from pharmacie ('apothecary art, pharmacy'), via Medieval Latin pharmacia from Ancient Greek pharmakeía ('preparation of remedies'), from phármakon ('medicinal herb, remedy').

pierre.etymology: Pierre comes from Latin petra ('rock, stone', borrowed from Ancient Greek pétra). Diphthongisation of open e to ie and lenition of -tr- to -rr- yielded Old French piere, pierre.
pierre.notes: Also the source of the first name *Pierre* ('Peter'); **en pierre** = made of stone.

pinceau.etymology: Inherited from Old French pincel, from Vulgar Latin *penicellus, a variant of Classical Latin penicillus ('painter's fine brush', originally 'little tuft of tail hair', double diminutive of penis 'tail').

piste.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally in horsemanship) from Italian pista ('beaten track left by hooves, trail'), feminine participial noun of Late Latin pistare ('to pound, tread down', frequentative of pinsere).

pièce.etymology: Pièce is traced to reconstructed Gaulish *pettia, a small piece. Its French history is recorded from the eleventh century. The theatre sense is one of several later uses of this general noun.

place.etymology: Place came through Latin platea from Greek plateia hodos, a broad street. The French noun is recorded from the eleventh century; its modern senses include a location, space or seat.

plafond.etymology: Originally spelled plat-fonds or plat fond in sixteenth-century architecture—literally 'flat bottom / flat underside' (plat 'flat' + fond 'bottom, background'), describing a flat boarded or plastered ceiling underside as opposed to an open arched vault. plaire.etymology: Plaire is a remodelling of the older French verb plaisir, itself descended from Latin placere, to be pleasing. The Académie dates plaire to the twelfth century.

plan.etymology: Plan blends two related Latin origins: planus ('flat, level surface', giving a flat architectural drawing or town map) and plantare ('to lay out on the ground'), expanding from a floor plan to any project or scheme.
plan.notes: **Un plan de la ville** = a city map; **un bon plan** = a good idea/deal.

pluie.etymology: Pluie comes from Popular Latin *ploia (for Classical Latin pluvia, 'rain', from pluere 'to rain'), matching Italian pioggia.
pluie.notes: Paired with the impersonal verb **pleuvoir** (*il pleut* = 'it is raining').

poids.etymology: Inherited from Old French peis / pois ('weight'), from Vulgar Latin pensum ('amount weighed out', neuter participle of pendere 'to hang on a scale, weigh'). Sixteenth-century humanists inserted a silent -d- in poids on the mistaken belief that it came from Latin pondus!

poids.notes: From the same Latin *pensare* ('to weigh carefully') come both **peser** ('to weigh') and **penser** ('to think—to weigh in the mind')!

point.etymology: Point descends from Latin punctum, a prick, tiny hole or dot, related to pungere, to prick. The Académie dates the noun to the eleventh century. Expressions such as au point extend the noun’s range.

pomme.etymology: Pomme comes from Late Latin poma (originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin pomum 'tree fruit', reinterpreted as a feminine singular). In French it narrowed specifically to the apple.

poncer.etymology: Derived from ponce ('pumice', in pierre ponce 'pumice stone', inherited from Latin pumicem). Before modern sandpaper, cabinetmakers smoothed wood and parchment by rubbing them with powdered pumice stone.

history.meaning: pumice -> to polish or smooth with pumice, then sandpaper

pont.etymology: Pont comes directly from Latin pons, pontis ('bridge'). Its accusative pontem regularly yielded Old French and modern French pont.
pont.notes: In French work life, **faire le pont** means taking a Friday or Monday off between a holiday and the weekend.

porcelaine.etymology: Borrowed via Italian porcellana (attested in Marco Polo's travels). In Italian porcellana first meant the smooth, glossy white cowrie shell (diminutive of porcella 'little sow', from a perceived shell shape); Europeans transferred the shell's name to translucent white Chinese ceramic with the same pearly lustre.

history.meaning: glossy white cowrie shell -> fine Chinese ceramic

porche.etymology: Inherited from Old French porche, from Classical Latin porticus ('colonnaded gallery, covered entrance porch'), derived from porta ('gate, entranceway').

porche.notes: In French towns, **un porche** often names the deep vaulted stone carriageway leading from the street into a quiet inner courtyard (**la cour**).

porte.etymology: Porte comes directly from Latin porta ('city gate, doorway'), sharing an Indo-European root for crossing or passing through with port ('harbour') and porter ('to carry').
porte.notes: Compare **le portail** ('large courtyard or driveway gate') from the same Latin family.

portrait.etymology: Substantivized past participle of Old and Middle French portraire ('to draw forth, trace line by line, depict'), inherited from Classical Latin protrahere ('to draw forward, bring to light': pro- + trahere 'to draw').

portrait.notes: Notice how **portrait** and **trait** share Latin *trahere* ('to draw a line'): hence the French idiom **tout le portrait de... / trait pour trait** ('the spitting image of...').

poser.etymology: Poser comes curiously from Late Latin pausare ('to pause, rest', from Greek paûsis 'cessation'), which in Romance took over the meanings of Classical Latin ponere ('to put, place') because of their similar past participles.
poser.notes: **Poser une valise** = to set down a suitcase; **poser une question** = to ask a question.

poterie.etymology: Formed in twelfth-century Old French from potier ('potter', itself from pot + -ier) plus the craft/collective suffix -ie. English pottery was borrowed directly from Old French poterie.

pouce.etymology: Inherited via Old French polce from Classical Latin pollex, pollicem ('thumb, big toe').

pouce.notes: Giving someone a gentle nudge forward with your thumb inspired **donner un coup de pouce** ('to lend a helping hand'), while playground truces cry **Pouce!** ('Time-out!').

poudre.etymology: Inherited via Old French polre -> poldre -> poudre (with regular glide consonant -d- inserted between -l- and -r-, followed by vocalization of -l- to -u-) from Classical Latin pulvis, pulverem ('dust, fine powder').

poudre.notes: In French baking, **sucre en poudre** is granulated/caster sugar (not icing sugar, which is **sucre glace**!), and **poudre d'amandes** is ground almonds.

pour.etymology: Pour continues Latin pro. The Académie records French pro in the ninth century, por and pur in the eleventh, and pour in the thirteenth.

pouvoir.etymology: Pouvoir descends from reconstructed Popular Latin *potere, a remodelling of Classical Latin posse, to be able. Earlier French forms included poeir before pouvoir became established.

prendre.etymology: Prendre comes from Latin prendere, a contracted form of prehendere, meaning to grasp or take. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. The idea of taking underlies its many extended senses.
prendre.notes: Very common: *prendre le petit-déjeuner*, *prendre une décision*, *prendre un bain*. Note the stem change: *il prend* but *ils prennent*.

presque.etymology: Presque developed from combinations involving the older French pres and que. The Académie records stages such as bien pres que and pres que before the words became the modern adverb.

printemps.etymology: Inherited from Spoken Latin *primum tempus ('first season, start of the fine weather', from primus 'first' + tempus 'time, season'), replacing Classical Latin ver. Fused in Old French as printens, later respelled printemps after temps.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: printemps (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

problème.etymology: Problème was borrowed through Latin problema from Greek problêma, something put forward and then a task or question. The French noun is recorded from the fourteenth century.

prochain.etymology: Prochain descends from reconstructed later Latin *propeanus, derived from prope, near. The French adjective is recorded from the twelfth century; its history connects next with nearness.

promenade.etymology: Formed in the 16th century with suffix -ade from promener ('to take for a walk, walk back and forth'), earlier Old French pormener (por- 'forth' + mener 'to lead' < Late Latin minare 'to drive/lead onward').

promenade.notes: **Une promenade** names both the act of strolling (**faire une promenade**) and the scenic tree-lined avenue itself.

proposer.etymology: Proposer was borrowed from Latin proponere, to place before someone or set forth. Its French shape was influenced by poser. The Académie records it from the twelfth century.

propriétaire.etymology: Propriétaire comes from Late Latin proprietarius ('owner of property', from proprietas 'ownership', built on proprius 'one's own').
propriétaire.notes: Same form for masculine and feminine (**le / la propriétaire**).

pupitre.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (pupiltre -> pupitre) from Classical Latin pulpitum ('wooden platform, reading stand, lectern'—the same Latin word that gave English pulpit).

pénible.etymology: Pénible is derived from peine, trouble or effort. The Académie dates the adjective to the twelfth century. It is not explained by simply assigning a generic meaning to the ending -ible.

pétrir.etymology: Inherited from Old French pestrir ('to knead dough'), from Late/Vulgar Latin *pisturire, built on Classical Latin pistura ('pounding grain, baking') and pistor ('baker', originally 'grain-pounder', from pinsere 'to crush, knead').
